Thanks to everyone who contributed and voted!

It's been a while! Sorry I had to concentrate on other items for a while. 

On arguments for GTFS-NewTrips or something similar, I wrote [this doc](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1EnRcD1Tytkn3zNIqFmVDCxs0hFcF5opMlKY8EgyZGiU/edit#heading=h.a1jl6pk4tg1) that explain why we think it's not a good idea or at least shouldn't replace TripModification. @doconnoronca 

On how we would define bus bridges, here is [my first proposal](https://github.com/TransitApp/transit/pull/11). It's far from finished but I think gives an idea on how this could work. @sam-hickey-ibigroup @bdferris-v2

I reviewed [your doc](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1EnRcD1Tytkn3zNIqFmVDCxs0hFcF5opMlKY8EgyZGiU/edit).

I see that what I had in mind has been considered.

File compactness: The amount of data required is still modest by modern internet standards and if it is in a separate feed that would only be checked occasionally it shouldn't be an issue.

Validation: Having less to validate is just the natural result of it being more flexible. Since the structure is similar to GTFS, similar validations could be applied.

Compatibility: Finding a way to be compatible with older systems depends on how you assume they handle unexpected data. Do they use the stop_id or stop_sequence? Do they ignore unrecognized trip_ids or try to include them in predictions?

I found that relying on perfect synchronicity between GTFS and GTFS-RT will not get you far. Dealing with unrecognized trip_ids is common due to things like sync problems between GTFS and GTFS-RT or agencies adding additional trips to the feed with or without using the schedule relationship added. As a result, when I tested the trip-modifications version of the Swiftly feed on TransSee, trips subject to modifications appeared in predictions twice. 

However the trip modifications are described, they either will need to have different trip_ids and the originals canceled or they will have to replace the original trip_ids.

Implementation clarity: The [GTFS-NewTrips](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1oPfQ6Xvui0g3xiy1pNiyu5cWFLhvrTVyvYsMVKGyGWM/edit#bookmark=id.v6hpeknwiyjm) proposal you linked or using Trip Updates closely matches the GTFS structure that consumers already have to support. That should make it easier to implement than the structure proposed in Trip-Modifications, where we have to process it in a new way to add it to our schedule data. Then further changes will be needed down the road to make it more flexible to support things like replacement shuttles.

The GTFS real-time specification already has an experimental specification for a Google encoded polylines. Having lines encoded using two different formats in the same specification is probably not a good idea.
That argument did not make it for GTFS-Flex.

At today's OpenTripPlanner (OTP) developer meeting, @leonardehrenfried mentioned that this proposal was moving along and it would be helpful to review and comment on it sooner rather than later.

These days I don't use GTFS-RT regularly as most of my GTFS use is in long term service planning. However I was responsible for one of the early GTFS-RT consumers capable of handling a large number of updates in a streaming fashion, and it is likely I'd contribute to the updates this proposal would require to the OTP realtime system.

I appreciate that this proposal focuses on a single concrete use case, and it seems like people have taken the time to work through the implications of different options, prioritizing a change that is particularly useful for riders.  Here are some observations in hopes that they'll be useful:

## A) Name

The word "modifications" can include a lot of things, while this proposal seems to be used almost exclusively for detours. TripDetours is both more specific and 6 characters shorter than TripModifications.

## B) Consumer Implementations

In response to the various comments on whether these change messages mesh well with specific routing algorithms https://github.com/google/transit/pull/403#issuecomment-1736446578 makes a very good point. Many (most?) people are using RT information to check on trips they already plan to take, or check the situation at their usual stop or on their usual route. Even if the effects on routing or trip planning are messy, these messages can always be used in post-processing itineraries to add alerts or sending updates to people already expecting to use the route. 

It's essential to consider the tractability of any implied consumer-side operations, but in this case I'm mostly concerned about the consistency and effectiveness of the data model in describing detours emerging in real time.

## C) Patterns

The concept of stop patterns appears in many GTFS consumers, but is not present in GTFS itself. An initial step when reading GTFS is often grouping the trips into "patterns" that pick up / drop off passengers at the same stops in the same order. These patterns are not materialized in the GTFS feed, so the source data is somewhat denormalized: The stop_times of many different trips will repeat the same stop_ids in the same order, though potentially with different stop sequence numbers and other information. If this concept is added to the spec, it should be done very intentionally and with a carefully chosen definition.

https://github.com/google/transit/pull/403#discussion_r1345818496
>It's the first time that concept is introduced in the spec indeed. We can define 'stop pattern' more completely, but I do feel it's a good concept to have in the spec.

The idea of stop patterns is introduced here almost as a footnote, with a very particular definition that is narrower than that used in many trip planners: it requires the stop sequence numbers on all the trips to be identical rather than just identically ordered. It seems like this definition of patterns is introduced solely to allow the replaced segment of the trip to be specified unambiguously in terms of stop sequence number and length, to avoid problems where the same stop appears more than once on a trip. 

Alternatives exist for specifying the detour segment in terms of stop_ids. This could be a full list of stop_ids on the replaced segment, or a beginning and end stop_id before and after the segment. As long as it is made clear that such a specification matches only the first instance on a given trip (or alternatively all instances), this would allow adding detours to a wide range of trips, even across several routes, with a single message.

https://github.com/google/transit/pull/403#issuecomment-1749335641
> We understand the benefit of grouping by trip_ids by stop patterns as noted in @gcamp’s reply in issue 369, but we have some concern about the inefficiencies or repeated data that will result from this requirement.

I agree. The downside of the stop sequence based segment selection is that it can only be applied to trips within a single stop pattern, using a new narrow definition of pattern given here, so separate messages may be needed for every pattern on every route passing through the same street. 

Rather than generating hundreds of modifications for all patterns on all routes running through a segment of a common trunk, it may be possible to select them with a single message per route, or even a single message across several routes if route_ids can be specified in addition to or in place of trip_ids.

## D) Unstructured IDs

https://github.com/google/transit/pull/403#issuecomment-1749606281
> The producer may provide TUs for the replacement trip ID (modifications_id + _ + trip_id).

GTFS-RT is using a structured binary data format, but this is multiplexing multiple identifiers into a single field using a delimiter character, which is also a valid character in both of the IDs. This feels like a hack to me, something that might be added after the fact to solve an unforeseen problem, but not in a newly created specification.

https://github.com/google/transit/pull/403#discussion_r1345843876
> Other ids having underscore should not create problem however since there's no need of parsing the id after it's been created.

It seems plausible one would want or need to parse out the modifications_id and trip_id on the consumer side. Even if this does not need to be parsed, there is a potential for name collisions. Consider a feed with trips A_B and B, and a modification with modifications_id A applying to trip B. Of course the naming scheme could be engineered to avoid collisions (even probabilistically using UUIDs), but consider merged feeds or feeds with simple identifiers. No one should need to design around accidentally causing collisions or name mangling in a newly created system - these should just be separate namespaces. What is the motivation for making it "stringly typed"?

It also jumps out at me that modifications_id is plural and applies to multiple modifications. I'm still working through the purpose of the nesting. Is this just an adaptation to the definition of stop patterns, and the need for many modifications to change all patterns on a route? If patterns and sequence numbers are not used, would this mostly collapse to a flat stream of messages, one ID per message?

Overall, this part of the proposal feels unfinished to me.

My initial reaction was similar to https://github.com/google/transit/pull/403#discussion_r1373858384
>But maybe this is all just hand-waving around my specific concern: I don't really like the "new trip id" = modifications_id + _ + trip_id convention. I'd rather put modification_id as a first-class field in TripDescriptor if you need that linkage. But why is this modification id needed here at all? 

Regarding the wording:

https://github.com/google/transit/pull/403#discussion_r1368993334
> to me, this is still confusing about whether the SHOULD applies to providing a TripUpdate or the trip ID format. Given the other locations which seem to indicate that the trip ID format is a MUST, this could be split into two sentences.

I agree that SHOULD/MUST terms apply separately to the presence of an identifier and the specific format used for that identifier. This should be clarified in the text.


## E) Deleting Detours

The question arose of how to remove a detour once it's been added, and was addressed in these comments:

https://github.com/google/transit/pull/403#issuecomment-1775563505
> Yes, the goal was to have the TripModifications removed from the feed, which should revert to the static GTFS state. Do you see any problem with this approach?

https://github.com/google/transit/pull/403#issuecomment-1775599271 
> It means we have to constantly check if there are any modifications that need to be removed.

This seems to assume `incrementality: FULL_DATASET`. How does this work with `incrementality: DIFFERENTIAL`? Are there any other parts of the RT spec that is not compatible with incremental streaming updates or would this be the first one?

> The word "modifications" can include a lot of things, while this proposal seems to be used almost exclusively for detours. TripDetours is both more specific and 6 characters shorter than TripModifications.

It also just occurred to me that TripModifications don't necessarily apply to trips, they may apply to entire stop patterns or entire routes. So instead of TripDetours, could these just be Detours? Maybe equally or more accurate in the context, and 10 characters shorter than TripModifications.

@doconnoronca 

I'm curious why you think file size doesn't matter. The NewTrips is orders of magnitude bigger and will cause bottlenecks in real time systems. TripUpdates are already reaching sizes of 5MB+ for example the feeds in New South Wales and NewTrip for high frequency lines has the possibility to be way higher than this. [Protobuf itself was chosen because of the file size it produces. ](https://github.com/google/transit/blob/master/gtfs-realtime/CHANGES.md#feeds-should-be-efficient-to-produce-and-consume-in-realtime)

> I found that relying on perfect synchronicity between GTFS and GTFS-RT will not get you far. [...]  As a result, when I tested the trip-modifications version of the Swiftly feed on TransSee, trips subject to modifications appeared in predictions twice.

I don't think we should be trying to fix that with this PR, even if I agree this is a problematic aspect of GTFS-rt. If you currently match trips with some match heuristic that's not with `TripDescriptor`, it can be updated to work with TripModifications. 

@abyrd 

### A) Name

Trip modifications can be more than just detours like as mentioned earlier there's other types of disruption that are very similar to detours but aren't detours like bus bridges. I'm not against a less generic name but it should be more generic than detours. The granularity of the selection is on the trip level, even if there’s enforcement that they all have the same stop pattern, so it’s not globally on route or stop pattern. For example, the STM in Montreal has rush hour detours that exist only on part of the day but on the same stop pattern that runs all day. 

### B) Consumer Implementations

I'm unsure of the point made here, but [our implementation](https://github.com/google/transit/pull/403#issuecomment-1737491942) is integrated in the trip planner. Even if other types of implementation are not able to do so, they could use Trip-Modifications as post-processing steps as you mention. Was that simply an observation more than something that needed fixing? 

### C) Patterns

I welcome proposals on how to achieve what we did without using the stop pattern concept, while keeping the ability to target stops on trips that re-use the same stops in the trip and avoid something very verbose like NewTrips. Targeting list of stops like you propose could work but wouldn’t work if reused stops aren’t having the same detour.

I see the value in stop patterns even as a 'local' concept specific to trip modifications, even if it is not currently used in GTFS. It's a simple concept that makes data representation efficient.

### D) Unstructured IDs

With more thoughts, we agree the concatenation of IDs is not ideal. [Here's a proposal](https://github.com/TransitApp/transit/pull/12) to remove it and use values in `TripDescriptor` instead. cc @sam-hickey-ibigroup @paulswartz @bdferris-v2 because you had similar comments 

### E) Deleting Detours

To be honest, we never took that into account since it's not part of the official spec even if I knew it was sometimes used. I see in the [previous discussions](https://docs.google.com/document/d/19Dy6afltgs1ebbxKQGX4jpzWHh--Iw4AOO_rtX1bQoc/edit#heading=h.giueiiu2ge3y) the alerts aren't supported in differential. However, I could see a simple path where a `TripModifications` would keep the same `modifications_id` but be modified to contain no value in the `modifications` list, effectively deleting it.

Thanks for catching this @ponlawat-w !

Yes, this seems like it should appear in `translation` rather than `feed_info`.

Since this is just an editorial correction without impacting any semantics, I propose that we don’t need to go through the voting process. If there are no other opinions, we can proceed to merge directly in a few days.

> A) Name
> Trip modifications can be more than just detours like as mentioned earlier there's other types of disruption that are very similar to detours but aren't detours like bus bridges. I'm not against a less generic name but it should be more generic than detours.

The proposed change seems to allow identifying sections of existing trips and replacing those segments with different stops and paths. This seems to match closely with the notion of "detour". I see a comment saying you want to use it for bus bridges, but the only other references I found to bus bridges were questioning how TripModifications would apply to bus bridges. For example https://github.com/google/transit/pull/403#issuecomment-1778267850 and https://github.com/google/transit/pull/403#issuecomment-1769581436. I may have missed your explanation because of how GitHub collapses comments, which makes it harder to search. Can you provide a link to the part of this proposal/discussion that explains how it would cover non-detour cases? 

Is it possible that non-detour cases are better covered by a cancel-and-replace strategy? If so, is the scope of this TripModification actually reduced to only detours/reroutes?

> B) Consumer Implementations
> I'm unsure of the point made here, but [our implementation](https://github.com/google/transit/pull/403#issuecomment-1737491942) is integrated in the trip planner.

Sorry if I was unclear. I was seeing many comments questioning whether details of TripModifications were compatible with specific routing algorithms. I was saying that even if it's challenging to apply these updates in certain routing consumers (it doesn't seem that bad for ones I'm familiar with), they clearly seem to represent a concept operators want to communicate to their riders (bus X will take this partially different route this afternoon). People may often see this via a non-routing centric system like a display or monitoring app. So better to help operators communicate it, and in the worst case the messages can be treated like alerts if someone can't incorporate them into the routing.

> C) Patterns
> I welcome proposals on how to achieve what we did without using the stop pattern concept, while keeping the ability to target stops on trips that re-use the same stops in the trip and avoid something very verbose like NewTrips. Targeting list of stops like you propose could work but wouldn’t work if reused stops aren’t having the same detour.

Stops may of course appear multiple times in a trip. Stop sub-sequences are more unique. And if a stop sub-sequence `A-B-C-D-E` or the bookend representation `A-*-E` or `A-?-?-?-E` is rerouted, is it reasonable to assume that all instances of that sub-sequence would be subject to the same rerouting? In the vast majority of cases a non-trivial (>1 stop) sub-sequence would not appear more than once, so it would work to match only the first instance of the sub-sequence in each trip?

> I see the value in stop patterns even as a 'local' concept specific to trip modifications, even if it is not currently used in GTFS. It's a simple concept that makes data representation efficient.

I definitely see the value as a concept in GTFS. But it is so central to GTFS and how consumers interpret GTFS that I don't think it should be introduced as a convenience adapted to one specific RT extension, which could clash with pre-existing implicit ideas of stop patterns, or later explicit addition of stop patterns to GTFS. Introducing it requires every consumer and producer to implement this particular TripModifications definition of stop patterns, and perform sort and group operations on that basis, alongside any existing analogous but different definitions and operations. 

I get the opposite impression you do: employing patterns makes the representation less efficient (more voluminous), requiring one message per pattern instead of a single message modifying any number of routes or trips via stop_id sub-sequence matching.

In this case use of patterns seems to fragment what are often inherently route-oriented updates into one per pattern, with exhaustive lists of trips, and possibly contribute to or lead to the nesting of many update messages under a single ID.

> D) Unstructured IDs
> With more thoughts, we agree the concatenation of IDs is not ideal. [Here's a proposal](https://github.com/TransitApp/transit/pull/12) to remove it and use values in `TripDescriptor` instead. cc @sam-hickey-ibigroup @paulswartz @bdferris-v2 because you had similar comments

In the protobuf definition, is the trip_id in the outer TripDescriptor repeated in the inner ModifiedTripSelector as affected_trip_id? If so, wouldn't this sub-message format equivalent to just adding the optional modifications_id to the outer TripDescriptor message? 

If a modifications_id is actually needed in TripUpdates, adding it to the protobuf at the TripDescriptor (or possibly ModifiedTripSelector) level this way seems preferable to string concatenation. But I'm still trying to work out why the TripUpdates wouldn't just reference the original trip ID, with detour and TripUpdate both applied cumulatively on top of the schedule. I will need to retrace the previous discussion more closely to fully understand this.

> E) Deleting Detours
> To be honest, we never took that into account since it's not part of the official spec even if I knew it was sometimes used. I see in the [previous discussions](https://docs.google.com/document/d/19Dy6afltgs1ebbxKQGX4jpzWHh--Iw4AOO_rtX1bQoc/edit#heading=h.giueiiu2ge3y) the alerts aren't supported in differential.

@doconnoronca wrote:
> File compactness: The amount of data required is still modest by modern internet standards and if it is in a separate feed that would only be checked occasionally it shouldn't be an issue.

I generally agree with your observations on pros and cons of cancel-and-add (or cancel-and-modify) versus the proposed TripModifications. I can see an argument for just using cancel-and-add over a special-purpose detour (TripModifications) message. Particularly when the TripModifications operate at a special intermediate level of abstraction which is the stop-pattern-including-stop-sequence-numbers, so still require a lot of processing and multiple nested messages to get the job done. But the TripModifications do help with compactness, and especially if they are made more general (apply to entities larger than stop-sequence-patterns such as routes) this compactness could be a real advantage.

I think it's worth aiming for compactness when possible. A few thoughts on data volume:

- Realtime messages may need to be distributed to embedded devices or over legacy or weak mobile networks. 
- Since we're using protobuf, compact messaging seems to be an obvious consideration
- Transport network size and update frequency varies greatly. The amount of data is significant in countries with unified passenger information systems and updates streaming in from every vehicle every few seconds.

But "volume is significant" is still way to vague. The importance probably won't be clear unless we work from requirements: what's the slowest network over which these messages need to be delivered? What's the bandwidth already consumed by polling/streaming of all non-detour updates on the largest networks we know of? What's the largest volume of individual trip cancel-and-add messages that would be simultaneously active for detours at a national or metropolitan scale? What volume of data does that represent relative to the volume of data for all messages on the entire network?

It also matters that I tend to look at this from a differential/incremental update perspective. In differential mode, the cancel-and-add detour messages would be very infrequent and possibly negligible in the total data volume. In full-dataset polling mode, they would appear in every polling response and could make up a large percentage of the data.

## First Producer/Consumer Example: Helsinki, Finland to OpenTripPlanner
This is not the oldest example (which dates back to 2013) but a more recent example for which we have ample documentation.

### Producers: HSL (Helsinki) and Digitransit (Finland)
Helsingin seudun liikenne (HSL) is the Helsinki Regional Transport Authority. Digitransit is the open-source trip planner they began building in 2016 together with Fintraffic (covering the rest of Finland). 

Here is a Github repository for the HSL realtime component: https://github.com/HSLdevcom/transitdata
Its readme contains a large diagram of the whole system: ![HSL System Diagram](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HSLdevcom/transitdata/master/transitdata_data_flow_drawio.png) The output MQTT brokers visible at the top edge of the diagram. The one on the left `cmqttdev.cinfra.fi` shows a topic `gtfs/rt/dev/fi/hsl/vp` which is VehiclePositions. The one on the right `pred.rt.hsl.fi` shows a family of topics `gtfsrt/[dev|v2]/fi/hsl/[tu|sa]` which are the trip updates and service alerts. Note that these are HSL-specific brokers and provide information only on HSL services.

More information on the HSL realtime data flow is provided here: https://github.com/HSLdevcom/digitransit/blob/master/Dataflows.md#realtime-data-flow

The Digitransit brokers cover everything "not HSL", with a breakdown into feeds documented at https://digitransit.fi/en/developers/apis/4-realtime-api/vehicle-positions/digitransit-mqtt/#available-cities-and-regions 
Documentation should be updated soon, as these now include the national trains as well as a subset of local trains operating in the HSL area. 

The division into multiple brokers is apparently for historical reasons. HSL has had its own brokers for over 7 years, and the newer Digitransit MQTT broker is an extension funded by the other participants in the project.

#### Connecting to Sources
The topics on the HSL brokers *do not* have a leading slash and will close the connection if you add one. The HSL brokers seem to accept only unencrypted mqtt connections on port 1883. The topics on the Digitransit brokers **do** have a leading slash. Digitransit brokers accept the mqtts (secure) protocol on port 8883, or unencrypted mqtt on port 1883.

To see a feed of TripUpdates for the Helsinki region on the HSL broker:
`mqtt subscribe -h pred.rt.hsl.fi -p 1883 -t "gtfsrt/v2/fi/hsl/tu" | xxd -c 32`

To see a feed of ServiceAlerts for the Helsinki region on the HSL broker:
`mqtt subscribe -h pred.rt.hsl.fi -p 1883 -t "gtfsrt/v2/fi/hsl/tu" | xxd -c 32`

To see a feed of VehiclePosition for one of the non-HSL feeds (here, Tampere) on the Digitransit broker:
`mqtt subscribe -h mqtt.digitransit.fi -p 1883 -t "/gtfsrt/vp/tampere/#" | xxd -c 32`

#### Upstream Use of GTFS-RT
If you trace the data flow diagram back from host `cmqttdev.cinfra.fi` topic `gtfsrt/dev/fi/hsl/vp` the data are coming from another MQTT broker `mqtt.hsl.fi` providing HFP messages. Upstream those are being translated from Matkahuolto GTFS-RT. So these HSL vehicle positions seem to be translated from GTFS-RT to HFP back to GTFS-RT, but using individual message passing for the whole "signal chain".

### Consumer: OpenTripPlanner
Digitransit is running a national-scale trip planner which autoscales computation nodes running OTP. Typically there are around 50 instances subscribing to the MQTT broker at once, with three external applications also subscribing. In September 2018 via https://github.com/opentripplanner/OpenTripPlanner/pull/2516#issuecomment-420348483 OpenTripPlanner gained the ability to consume incremental GTFS-RT TripUpdate messages over MQTT as opposed to websockets. The configuration I used for testing is here: https://github.com/HSLdevcom/OpenTripPlanner-data-container/blob/v3/hsl/router-config.json#L180 but I removed the parking and bicycle updaters.

#### End-to-End Data Rate

I instrumented an OpenTripPlanner instance to count bytes, messages, and updates received and let it run for about  24 minutes. The average data rate was 34kB/sec with 33 messages per second, each containing one TripUpdate. 

These match figures supplied by HSL: an average of 25 messages per second over the whole day, reaching 50 messages per second or higher at rush hour. Between 7AM and 7PM the range is typically 30-50 messages per second.

Note that at these rates, the whole unfiltered stream could in theory be carried on EDGE and definitely on 3G.

### Sources:
Interview on OpenTripPlanner developer chat with HSL employee @optionsome on 2023-12-13.
Previous Github comments from @hannesj (who no longer works for HSL).
Digitransit and HSL documentation.

## Second Producer/Consumer: Kirin and Kraken in Ile-de-France (Paris Region)

Navitia is a public transit passenger information system created by CanalTP, then Kisio Digital, then Hove. Many of its components are open source, and the whole system has been provided as a hosted service by these companies. This service backs various user-facing trip planner applications including ViaNavigo from Paris regional transit authority Ile-de-France Mobilités.

The Navitia system is quite complex. It’s not just the route optimization component, but includes the entire data integration pipeline for schedules and realtime data that feed into the router. Communication of transit data within this pipeline is via “enriched” GTFS and GTFS-RT.

As of this year, development of Navitia is no longer open. Apparently the copyright holders decided to stop licensing the codebase under the Affero GPL, but the previous versions of the source code are still accessible. There is an architecture overview on the main Navitia readme and the project wiki:
https://github.com/hove-io/navitia#architecture-overview
https://github.com/hove-io/navitia/wiki/Architecture

![Kirin and Chaos feed GTFS-RT to Kraken](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hove-io/navitia/dev/documentation/diagrams/Navitia_full_architecture.png)

Both of these show two modules called Kirin and Chaos handling realtime and service disruptions data, which pass through a message broker and on to the Kraken public transport routing component. Here are some repositories that demonstrate the use of GTFS and GTFS-RT by the Navitia pipeline including Chaos and Kirin:
https://github.com/hove-io/transit_model
https://github.com/hove-io/chaos-proto

We have a statement in a comment above at https://github.com/google/transit/issues/84#issuecomment-350393354 from a CanalTP employee in 2017 stating that Navitia realtime handling exactly corresponds to the GTFS-RT approach I have described, that this approach was adopted after discussing it with me personally, and that this approach is effective in leveling load. In all discussions I’ve had with Navitia developers over the years, my impression is that this system continues to function in the same way, with individual messages being applied at the trip level in a stream against the scheduled trips.

The case of Navitia is a bit ambiguous because the message-oriented, differential use of GTFS-RT is arguably within a single system, but it’s between two separate open source components of that system. It is used at a scale that we would often associate with an agency realtime integration pipeline producing data separately from consumer passenger information apps, but my sense is that both roles have been contracted out to a single entity here. 

While the main regional realtime system is SIRI-based, my understanding is that it is similarly incremental message-based, and is interconnected with GTFS-RT based systems upstream and at the final integration and routing stages. Several years back I vouched for the differential message passing approach during the design of this regional system, and I heard from a participant in the design process that this approach was adopted. So this regional SIRI-based system may arguably be inspired by how GTFS-RT was used in the Netherlands and other countries, as well as in Navitia itself.

While I don't have a diagram, I can speak to how MBTA is using `DIFFERENTIAL` GTFS-RT. At the moment, we're using MQTT and only for VehiclePositions. For each set of GPS updates, we publish a `DIFFERENTIAL` feed with those updates. Periodically (currently every 60s) we publish a `FULL_DATASET` feed as the "retained" message for the queue, allowing new clients to receive a full, if slightly stale, dataset. This also handles deletions for us, by removing offline vehicles from the `FULL_DATASET` feed. The code is available in https://github.com/mbta/concentrate, but the relevant bit is [here](https://github.com/mbta/concentrate/blob/master/lib/concentrate/merge/table.ex#L21-L40) where we distinguish between a `partial_update` (only updates the items specified in the feed) and a regular `update` where we remove the existing state first.

## Example 3: OpenOV to OpenTripPlanner (Netherlands)

This last example is the oldest one, dating back ten years to 2013. This is the original streaming message-oriented GTFS-RT system, and perhaps the first ever large scale open realtime data feed. 

### Producer

The Nationale Database Openbaar Vervoer (NDOV, "National Public Transport Database") is a government-run service in the Netherlands combining timetable, realtime, and fare data for use in trip planning services. Up until 2013 there was only one authorized subscriber which was a commercial trip planning API, and access to the raw data was very expensive. Stichting OpenGeo’s OpenOV project changed this situation by creating a second national-scale travel information service, thereby gaining access to the NDOV raw data in the local BISON Koppelvlak (KV) formats and republishing it in open standard formats. Over time the OpenOV GTFS feeds were recognized as the highest quality feeds for the Netherlands. They have since become the feeds consumed by Google for example.

At that time over 3000 vehicles were already monitored at any given moment, producing positions and arrival time predictions with updates on average every 10 seconds. It took around 2 seconds for a position to propagate from the vehicle down to stop arrival time predictions. The only way to handle this volume of information while preserving the low latency and high update frequency was to stream individual messages.

### Consumer

Emergence of this feed is what pushed OpenTripPlanner to originally add support for realtime trip updates. This means that OpenTripPlanner realtime trip update support has _always_ been differential message-oriented. Although OTP had support for realtime alerts as early as 2011, the first mentions of realtime trip updates in the OTP commit log date to the summer of 2012, with commit https://github.com/opentripplanner/OpenTripPlanner/commit/1fdb5a6615945cce831d2a39055c4aa83525cb6c (2012-06-21) applying Dutch KV8 data (analogous to GTFS-RT) from a ZeroMQ broker. This was quickly followed by draft GTFS-RT handlers and revisions to allow cleanly updating stoptimes concurrently with active search threads.

By a year later in the summer of 2013 we see commit https://github.com/opentripplanner/OpenTripPlanner/commit/d444bca0f8ed483d84c3f6b830c58dae6a12bde1 entitled “basic GTFS-RT over websockets”. What happened in between is the Multimodale Reisinformatie (MMRI, Multimodal Travel Information) project of the Dutch Transportation Ministry's "Beter Benutten" (Better Utilization) program. Three of the four consortia that participated in this pre-commercial research and development program were working with OpenTripPlanner, and one of those (https://github.com/bliksemlabs) created [R4](https://github.com/bliksemlabs/rrrr) which later inspired [R5](https://github.com/conveyal/r5), and in turn inspired the OpenTripPlanner 2 [transit routing engine](https://github.com/opentripplanner/OpenTripPlanner/tree/dev-2.x/src/main/java/org/opentripplanner/raptor).

Once the original OTP streaming realtime support had been built and demonstrated, the approach was described in this document: https://docs.google.com/document/d/19Dy6afltgs1ebbxKQGX4jpzWHh--Iw4AOO_rtX1bQoc  

### Current Status

As far as I know the MMRI message broker has been running since 2013 and has been used by various applications in the Netherlands. It is currently undergoing an overhaul to MQTT. More information should be available in the coming months.

> My bus bridge proposal was in [this](https://github.com/google/transit/pull/403#issuecomment-1832737691) message.

Thanks for the link. I do see how that fits in with the detour descriptions.

> > is it reasonable to assume that all instances of that sub-sequence would be subject to the same rerouting?
> 
> I think that's too generic of an assumption... [330 in Quebec City](https://www.rtcquebec.ca/horaires-et-trajets/horaires-des-bus/tous-les-parcours/330/univlaval-cegep-garneau) has a section where the same line take the same sequence of stop in both direction

I think we're not looking at this in the same way. In any given trip (not route), a non-trivial subsequence is very unlikely to occur more than once, and if it does you could just match all occurrences, or only the first one. On any particular trip, some stop sub-sequence should readily identify where to insert the detour. Can we find or construct any example where this is not the case? It would have to be a single trip that passes the same sequence of 2+ stops in the same order more than once. And even if such a case is found, an unambiguous detour can still be created by just replacing a longer super-sequence containing the two repeated subsequences.

The fact that a route like the 300 may contain different trips which use the same sub-sequence of stops in different ways is not what I'm referring to. If you want to affect only certain trips, then you'd select only those trips (either by listing out their IDs, or even by directionId if such a mechanism is provided). In the case where the detour does apply to every trip in all directions that pass through the subsequence, then you'd only need to provide the route ID.

I'm not fully convinced what I'm describing is "better", just pointing out we may not be talking about the same thing.

> Maybe the naming can be improved, but I don't think every consumer has the same definition of stop pattern and depending on your use, that definition can change depending on context. Generally, I don't think we can mandate one rule for every context.

I am not saying that every consumer has the same definition of stop pattern, or a single shared useful definition. That would be an argument in favor of adding stop patterns as a first-class concept in GTFS. I am not making that argument, I'm saying the opposite: it seems preferable _not_ to introduce this idea in this one specific form, as a way to apply only one specific kind of realtime update.

> > In the protobuf definition, is the trip_id in the outer TripDescriptor repeated in the inner ModifiedTripSelector as affected_trip_id?
> 
> One important goal (that was internally wanted to for us but @sam-hickey-ibigroup pushed heavily for too) is backward compatibility for old systems that don't know about modification.

I agree backward compatibility is of course a worthwhile goal, and I see how leaving out the trip_id would protect clients from messages about trips they don't realize have been modified (as long as they gracefully handle missing trip_ids). This becomes more widely useful if ModifiedTripSelector ends up referencing the more widely applicable FeedEntity ID instead of the more narrowly defined modifications_id: the ModifiedTripSelector could be used with future realtime message types. Something still feels a bit off to me, but I will need to think about this one more.
☝️ Yes. Or even better, this: https://github.com/google/transit/issues/127 (which could be easily used to generate the above)

By the way, I fully understand and appreciate that GTFS was created as the an antidote to “model entire world with angle brackets before implementing” traditional standardization processes like those of TCIP or NeTEx. People wanted to be able to create a stop without nesting XML 5 layers deep. But "formally defined data model" does not mean complex or unwieldy or excessive (as evidenced by DBML above).

GTFS started out as a CSV dump of a relational database at TriMet. People with some experience working with databases or data modeling tend to sense that and treat it as a relational model when discussing extensions. I think it benefits greatly from acknowledging that underlying structure.

At this point, the core of that specification has existed largely unchanged for a decade, and is used and directly or indirectly by millions of people. It’s no longer a handful of files from which every reader intuitively perceives the source structure.
I just created issue #415 to describe something that I think may be a major factor affecting timely review and comprehensive understanding of change proposals.

body: This is being worked on here: https://github.com/MobilityData/transit/pull/64

> ☝️ Yes. Or even better, this: #127 (which could be easily used to generate the above)

Thanks @e-lo for pointing that out. That ticket, and especially the comments on that ticket, are very related to what I'm proposing here. What I'm proposing is a bit stronger and has a different goal though, so I'd like to treat it as a separate issue.

I believe #127 is suggesting that the GTFS spec include, as an additional derived element or resource, a machine readable file for the specific purpose of generating source code to hold in-memory representations of GTFS data. In the present PR, I'm considering source code generation as a nice potential side effect but not the core purpose. I'm also proposing that we focus attention on the entity-relationship model itself, not the file that represents it, and give this model a very central role in GTFS, both technically and organizationally.

Regarding the problem statement that you and @dedavance listed in comments on that other issue in 
https://github.com/google/transit/issues/127#issuecomment-700299360 and
https://github.com/google/transit/issues/127#issuecomment-735904862
I generally agree, but with the following emphases and differences in the context of the present issue:

A) Data model as definitive or canonical source. In a comment on the other issue you said:
https://github.com/google/transit/issues/127#issuecomment-754297300
> I'm also interested in if the community would be amenable to using this type of definition as the canonical GTFS definition such that we can generate Markdown/HTML from the programatic definition in JSON rather than visa-versa.

This is exactly what I'm talking about. The key idea being that the model _is_ the source of truth, not just another derived artifact to be manually maintained in the spec. And to the extent that something like for example protobuf definition files can't be generated or patched directly from the entity-relationship model language, they should be derived by hand using the most mechanical or automatic process possible. Anything that emerges as non-obvious in this derivation should be clarified in the data model as the source of truth, not in the downstream artifacts.

B) The data model is equally central to GTFS, GTFS-RT, GTFS change proposals, and GTFS-RT change proposals. 
Proposals and discussions in all these places would primarily or at least initially concern changes to the data model, and which aggregates within that model are serialized as files or messages.

C) I'm suggesting that the governance and amendment process (currently under discussion in #413) be modified to take this into account. For example, an initial change proposal might consist of _only_ a use case description and a patch to the data model. People would discuss and vote on _only the data model change_ first, before anyone invested time in the minutiae of serialization into text files. Everyone would be looking at and discussing a single visual image. The rest of the process would need to be tweaked accordingly, this is just the initial idea.

I think GTFS has reached a size and complexity, both technically and in community structure, where its maintenance and viability may depend on this kind of formalization.

I'm starting to feel like this is almost a precondition for me to even participate in the change process. It is genuinely exhausting to reverse-engineer what personal data model each person has in their heads when reading each comment, and to try to describe fragments of that data model in text over and over, trying to determine whether one's own model matches others. Frequently I get the impression we are proceeding in the absence of even a mental data model, so the long-term coherence and stability of the spec will rely on the sheer chance of someone showing up at the right moment to infer and verify this shifting ghost of an idea.

After a discussion with @tzujenchanmbd:
- we've kept file requirements details in the **Dataset Files** section only
- added a mention of what "field" exists in the **Term Definitions** section to clarify what it is

I have modified the descriptive text back to using "exists" and not "defined" in [Change defined -> exists](https://github.com/google/transit/pull/414/commits/e013c7c9bf0a3821e21ddc8d1d22d70604f44222).

**We would like to thank everyone who took the time to review the proposed phasing plan and we are encouraged by your excitement! 🙏**

We are currently working on Phase 1 with some of the features being finalized as we speak. 

### Clarifications on Voting in Phase 2 
@e-lo  @westontrillium 

_Vote before testing with Veto_

- By placing the veto before the testing phase, we aim to increase reviews and discussions earlier in the process, leading to a more predictable testing phase. Verifying consensus at this stage allows for efficient resource management for both first consumers and producers. This approach reduces uncertainty and instills confidence in first producers and consumers during testing. 


_Vote for adoption with 80% threshold_

- We are hoping to increase the incentive to voting and reduce the effect of a veto at this stage.  

Additional details will be shared in a proposal to be published in early Q1 2024, including specifics on how this will impact the amendment process. We can anticipate the need for at least one Working Meeting to discuss and evaluate these voting changes. 

### Clarifications on Phase 3 - Fast-track process for smaller changes 
@gcamp  @e-lo  @leonardehrenfried 

While drafting this plan, we identified that Phase 3 is dependent on phase 2 so, we can  expect a proposal for this after the adoption of Phase 2. 
The idea is to distinguish between "large" and "small" changes. Certains changes may not need to be tested by a producer and a consumer, or even need a vote. 

How would you differentiate a normative vs non-normative change, a smaller or a bigger change? How would you name them?


### The GTFS Digest
@mmorang  @AdrianaCeric 

We plan to release the Digest in the upcoming week, offering more comprehensive details upon release. It will be available on a publicly accessible Google Group with a subscription option. Expect a monthly release around the mid-month mark, featuring updates on GTFS development and information on new specification adoptions. The appropriate channels will be used for promotion (i.e. LinkedIn, Slack, GitHub, ... ) 

We also have other locations for GTFS updates that are currently available: 

* [GTFS.org - Changes](https://gtfs.org/schedule/changes/) : Recent Changes to the spec with a short description
* [GTFS.org - Revision History](https://gtfs.org/schedule/process/#revision-history) : A history of recently adopted changes
* [GTFS-Changes Google Group](https://groups.google.com/g/gtfs-changes): An announcement board for changes as decribed in the current amendment process. 

We understand that these may not be optimized at the moment but we hope to improve their visibility and quality soon. 

As for videos on “YouTube”, we really like the idea but we see this as something we might want to do once the governance phasing plan is accomplished. At the moment, we do not have the capacity to do both but we will put in the future considerations.

### Flexibility in 1 Consumer and 1 Producers testing requirements and depreciation of “small” unused fields
@gcamp  @skinkie 

This is a very interesting proposal that we can either bring up during phase 3 discussions or place it in the future considerations sections. 

### Trial period for voting changes
@westontrillium 

This is interesting. How do you see this work in practice?

>Trial period for voting changes
>@westontrillium

>This is interesting. How do you see this work in practice?

This is *sort of* what happens in realtime now with experimental fields...which technically allow removal w/out undoing backwards compatibility but this hasn't been done in practice that I am aware of.

Straw person for implementation:

1. Approval of change doesn't require implementation, but a soft commitment to implement.
2. Trial period starts after approval and ends after implemented by a producer and consumer at which point this flag is removed.
3. Trial period can *expire* after 1 year after which it will either be removed or renewed by another vote.
4. ❓ Could changes be made during the trial period if implementers find an issue?

>Vote before testing with Veto
> By placing the veto before the testing phase, we aim to increase reviews and discussions earlier in the process, leading to a more predictable testing phase. Verifying consensus at this stage allows for efficient resource management for both first consumers and producers. This approach reduces uncertainty and instills confidence in first producers and consumers during testing.

I'm still not clear about what this process looks like.  Are you saying that the initial vote would require unanimity?  That seems like a tall order when you don't know necessarily what you are approving.

@eliasmbd @e-lo Sorry if I was unclear. What I mean is a trial period of the voting process *itself*, i.e., there is an agreement to implement the voting process as a provisional change and then have a sort of referendum vote at the end of that period deciding if we lock in the new process or revert to the original. The assumption I'm going on is that there is inherent risk in immediately fully committing to any untested change in process. Maybe that risk is minimal, maybe any change is better than the status quo, but we won't really know how a new voting process will work out until we implement it and that gives me some pause.

For what it's worth, my first impression of the proposed voting process change is definitely positive, I just want to make sure we approach such a change intelligently.

**Edit: I realize I forgot to actually provide an example. One way it could work in practice is:**
1. Initial vote
- New voting process discussed, proposal finalized, a vote takes place to adopt it
  - The initial vote has the provision that the new process is effective from X date to, say, two years from X date.

2. Trial period
- MobilityData tracks pain points, successes, failures, gaps, etc., and encourage community members to commit to doing the same. All votes during this period are considered valid beyond the trial period, regardless of outcome of the referendum vote.

3. Referendum vote
- Use the collectively gathered data, anecdotal or otherwise, to help determine if this change was actually an improvement.
- MobilityData calls a vote on whether to officially adopt this new process or revert back to the original and open the discussion for alternative improvements to the process.

>@eliasmbd @e-lo Sorry if I was unclear. What I mean is a trial period of the voting process itself 

OoooooOOOOooo.  Gotcha :-) (finally)

Adding a clarification after @e-lo 's comment:
> That seems like a tall order when you don't know necessarily what you are approving.

This first vote would be called in the Pull Request, with the exact spec changes & all additional documentation going with a proposed change. Looking at examples of PRs, this initial vote could happen:
- [at this stage](https://github.com/google/transit/pull/355#issuecomment-1430617967) for #355.
- [at this stage](https://github.com/google/transit/pull/286#issuecomment-990258396) for #286.

Note that we are also working on integrating review guidelines in the same phase to make it easier for contributors to review and further increase chances of identifying issues that might remain.

Upon the outcome of this vote, the proposal advances to the testing phase, during which we require the presence of at least 1 producer and 1 consumer to incorporate the latest changes, with more confidence that major risks have been identified. (This could be the opportune time to also update the canonical validator!)
We could define what changes are accepted as a result of the testing phase without going back to the first vote (e. g. needs a small clarification or a change to a field name).

Although this might partially address the **_Insufficient engagement in the proposals in the early stages of development_** problem, this is mainly intended to address the **_First adopters are frequently impacted by last-minute changes to their implementation, leading to an increase in committed resources_** problem.
We anticipate that other solutions will primarily address the early engagement before the PR stage, such as the GTFS Digest publication, a better use of GitHub features on this repo, a change to the spec amendment process to better represent all the ways one can contribute ([example](https://github.com/MobilityData/gtfs-validator/blob/master/docs/CONTRIBUTING.md#ways-to-contribute)).

Now you might be wondering: why do we even need a second vote then? This is a good question 🙂.

**In [GBFS](https://gbfs.org/specification/process/)**, changes are voted in several PRs to be part of a Release Candidate. The Release Candidate becomes an official Release when the changes are implemented in production (a Release Candidate becoming official is as [as simple as this](https://github.com/MobilityData/gbfs/commit/b7d8163704f8682fd2a8ab978a1cafdee4e1abbd)). Small editorial changes can happen during the Release Candidate phase based on community feedback. 

**In [GTFS Realtime](https://gtfs.org/realtime/process/#adding-new-fields-to-gtfs-realtime)**, a first vote occurs to add a field as _experimental_. This first vote needs unanimous consensus yes with at least 3 votes ([example](https://github.com/google/transit/pull/136)).
Then, a second PR can be opened to change the field status to _official_. This second vote needs 80% yes ([example](https://github.com/google/transit/pull/214)). 
An experimental field is _in theory_ deprecated if not officially adopted within 2 years (which joins @skinkie 's [comment](https://github.com/google/transit/issues/413#issuecomment-1854288342)), although not done in practice as @e-lo pointed out.

These have the advantage of having longer testing periods. That being said, keeping the two "steps" (1- we think this is a good idea and 2- it works in practice) inside one single PR has the advantage of making the changes resulting from testing immediately and retaining a certain simplicity. Additionally, longer test periods don't necessarily mean stronger testing: we also could imagine requiring more than 1 producer and 1 consumer to implement changes.
The second vote could act as a final check on compliance with the amendment process.

Thoughts?

Agree with what you said @isabelle-dr in the previous message, one small thing is that I would make the first vote before the example given. Before any consumer or producer actually starts working on that. In Fares-v2 that would be even before [an issue would be open](https://github.com/google/transit/issues/252) (probably sometime after the initial feedback on the [google doc](https://docs.google.com/document/d/19j-f-wZ5C_kYXmkLBye1g42U-kvfSVgYLkkG5oyBauY/edit#heading=h.mhjuwqk2h5r3))

It could mean months or even years between the two votes, but I think that's ok.

body: Following here from https://github.com/google/transit/issues/409, sharing a bit more about the @mbta's experience with rail replacement buses: > Another possibility would be to mark a route to be part/replacement of another route. That way we could link those together and use the information to link the real-time alerts to both routes. We are doing exactly this via another extension we designed and implemented, _[multi_route_trips.txt](https://github.com/mbta/gtfs-documentation/blob/master/reference/gtfs.md#multi_route_tripstxt)_. In the example below from our [Needham Line route timetable](https://www.mbta.com/schedules/CR-Needham/timetable), Train 839 and Train 841 are actually part of a different `route_id` for the Providence/Stoughton Line (they continue on to another destination beyond Forest Hills), but because the trips are linked to the Needham Line via _multi_route_trips.txt_, we are able to show them on this webpage. A similar treatment is used if, say, a shuttle bus replaced a portion or whole of a Needham Line trip. We originally added the `trip_route_type` extension in order to be able to distinguish "replacement bus" trips with normal rail trips on the same `route_id`, however ultimately moved to using separate routes; having trips on both rail and bus `route_id`s stopping at shared `stop_id`s caused issues with more than one feed consumer. Perhaps this could be overcome with an addition to the spec, but backward-compatibility should be considered. In our case, using a distinct `route_id` also allows us to give the bus service route/text colors that match the replacing buses, as well as separate route names—particularly useful in situations when a single bus service replaces multiple rail routes.

body:
Thanks for your efforts to share the feedback you’ve received, and for your ideas on the specification change process.
In principle, the idea of voting early on proposed changes makes sense to me, as does a more uniform process between scheduled and realtime GTFS specifications. However, after reading all the above comments, I still have some questions about what this would look like in practice, and questions about some underlying assumptions.

a) How complete does the early proposal need to be? Can it be only a concept (in an extreme example, a single sentence)? Or at the opposite extreme, does it need to include a full description of all changes to file formats, or a full description of changes to the underlying data model those file formats represent? Are these descriptions required to be complete, clear, or readily approachable by people who will not actually use them but must evaluate their suitability for inclusion in the spec? For example, are there requirements for visualizations or summary tables of some kind?

b) How close does this early description need to be to the final form at the later vote? For example, if the early proposal adds one optional field to a CSV file, can this be followed by a vote on a final proposal that adds a whole new file and requried fields? At what point is this not the same proposal?

c) Is the first vote actually required to precede any prototyping or testing? What if a proposal is made based on an existing prototype or de facto usage?

The idea of the early vote seems to be based on the premise that people or organizations plan changes in advance and seek approval for those ideas or plans before implementing them (even in a preliminary way for testing). My sense is that in practice, people build prototypes almost immediately from loose specifications and move on very quickly to using them, sometimes even in production in local regions, which is only later followed by a move to “get it into the spec”. I'm not saying there's anything inherently bad about this approach, I’m just describing what I see. Building a prototype and confronting it with practical use is a good way to develop and refine one’s ideas and get them into a workable state that can inform a later specification change proposal.

Are these standardization process changes intended to induce changes in existing development practices that (at least in the GTFS world) are generally iterative and fast-moving? If not, is there a possibility of divergence between software development and standardization, where the standardization process feigns an early approval and testing period, while in practice software development has already moved on to production use and will experience exactly the same tension between a locally suffcient implementation and broader community expectations for changes to a global standard?
 
Put differently, is the difficulty with proposing changes truly one of timing, or just that participants in the process don’t have the time and budget to work on a standardization process, as they’ve often only been hired to make something that works for their own use case or their own customers, and up to project or organization-specific quality expectations?

@gcamp wrote:
> * The "must be implemented by one producer and one consumer" rule is a good rule in spirits, but I think should be more flexible, especially for individual fields when adding a new normative change.

What would be the underlying reason for removing this requirement for one producer and one consumer? What is the advantage of adding things to the specification that have never actually been used to produce or consume data?

I'm not opposing any discussion of changes to the rule. I just genuinely don't know what the intended outcome is here.

> What would be the underlying reason for removing this requirement for one producer and one consumer? What is the advantage of adding things to the specification that have never actually been used to produce or consume data?

From my perspective the one to one relationship will still create private extensions between two parties. I am not at all happy that one actual data exchange would justify extending the schema, without a requirement for any other party to implement it.

> What would be the underlying reason for removing this requirement for one producer and one consumer?

@abyrd I wouldn't remove it but make it more flexible. Concrete examples : 
- Text to speech has been added to `tts_stop_name` but not other fields. Even if there's clearly a benefit on adding tts fields  on route name fields and headsigns, because there was only a stop `tts_stop_name` [producer at the time of the vote](https://github.com/google/transit/pull/49#issuecomment-561825216).
- GTFS-flex : mean_duration_factor, mean_duration_offset, safe_duration_factor, safe_duration_offset fields aren't used by any consumer (mainly because shortcuts were used in the implementation). Everyone agrees that the fields themselves are useful. Should we don't include those fields and have a spec with a clear 'hole' in it? 
- A situation I clearly see happening in the future : frequencies.txt are often not supported or badly supported by consumer. If there's a proposal for a new feature that doesn't support frequencies without adding a new field that won't be used. Should that feature not support frequencies at all? 
- (edit) This is the prefect example of a change I don't think should require a producer/consumer https://github.com/google/transit/issues/424

> The idea of the early vote seems to be based on the premise that people or organizations plan changes in advance and seek approval for those ideas or plans before implementing them (even in a preliminary way for testing).

That's what is happening a lot of time, that's what happened with pathways and with fares-v2. With Trip-Modifications we had an internal version but we [asked for comments](https://github.com/google/transit/issues/369) before Swiftly started implementation. 

I agree with small changes it often start internal, but if standardisation is a goal from the start, having a way to reduce risk of late and expensive change just before the final vote is really valuable.
These are all editorial changes and do not need a vote, although comments from the community are welcome! I will leave this PR open for a few days.

Phase 1 as been marked as done with the completion of [labels](https://github.com/google/transit/labels).

Currently, proposed changes to governance are not reflected in the existing labels. Modification of labels is a possibility as governance undergoes changes.

Moving forward, MobilityData will shift its attention to Phase 2 and draft a proposal. Your input, as outlined in the comments above, will be taken into consideration, and we are committed to keeping you actively involved. More information to come.

[Transit](https://transitapp.com/) follows this rule and has included it in its [Guidelines for producing GTFS static data](https://resources.transitapp.com/article/458-guidelines-for-producing-gtfs-static-data-for-transit#publishnew) for Transit's partners.

The main reason is GTFS data consumption is not an instantaneous process. At best it can take a couple of hours, but it can certainly take longer. Moreover, errors might occur (either in data production or data consumption) and this will require human intervention (and hence, some time) to resolve them. At a scale where a trip-planner application consumes hundreds of datasets, it happens every day. Having a few days as a buffer time between the moment the dataset is released and the moment the schedules are active helps a lot in displaying the new schedules on time, any time. We are not against consuming changes last-minute but IMHO, it shouldn't be the golden rule and should be reserved for urgent fixes.

@doconnoronca think about the situation where a producer has to maintain multiple GTFS-RT publications, while there is currently no recommendation to resolve the GTFS-RT URL for a specific version of the feed. If you as a producer assume that with publishing the latest version of your timetable has been exported, and therefore will not include any alterations in your GTFS-RT feed, it is likely that any consumer that did not proces the latest version will not have that change. Now in case the situation exists where there is a newer GTFS file and the GTFS-RT _would_ contain the alternation, it would not really make sense either. There are more issues at play here, and some operators actually have _versioned_ GTFS-RT running.

Thanks @gcamp for the meeting summary. 

I would like to clarify something that I have mentioned in comments above and (admittedly very poorly) tried to express in the recent meeting:

Referencing my comment above (https://github.com/google/transit/pull/403#issuecomment-1855880596)
>  even if such a case is found, **an unambiguous detour can still be created by just replacing a longer super-sequence**...

As I understand it, ambiguous sequences of stop IDs, including the minimal case of single stop, are not problematic. 

First, we do all agree on these two facts: a) stop_ids may certainly appear more than once in a trip; b) detours certainly exist that affect sections as short as a single stop on a trip. 

In the vast majority of cases, the sequence of stops affected by a detour will either be totally unique within each affected trip, or will be affected in exactly the same way each time it appears. The small fraction of remaining cases may be largely theoretical, but there is another thing we all agree upon: it is nonetheless important to identify and close any such theoretical gap, ensuring the system has complete and understandable semantics.

This gap is closed in the following way: ambiguity can always be eliminated by simply making the segment-selector and the corresponding detour longer, until it is no longer ambiguous. 

For example, if a route contains a loop with the stop sequence A-B-C-D-E-B-F (illustrated below). A detour is for some reason causing the bus to bypass the stop B and instead stop at replacement stop X, but only in the horizontal direction between A and C, and not in the vertical direction between E and F. It is sufficient to simply specify the detour as affecting segment A-B or B-C or A-B-C instead of just B (replaced with A-X or X-C or A-X-C respectively), and the ambiguity is gone. 

![Untitled-2024-01-18-1600](https://github.com/google/transit/assets/112871/6efa5aff-ad56-4caf-8cc9-ccdb542dfa11)

In this way, the stop-id-sequence ambiguity problem is trivially avoidable in every possible case, so long as the proposed TripModifications update type does not include a rule requiring the shortest possible representation of any detour, or a rule against detours including unchanged stops. The fact that there is always a solution of this form is clear from the maximal example: you can always specify a detour *for the entire sequence of stopIds in the trip* including the repeating parts. 

The situations in which the replaced segment may be ambiguous, as well as the way of making sure it is not ambiguous, seem intuitively clear and understandable to anyone producing data, with only a short comment in a best practices guide to explain this.

---

All of that said, please note that I am not inherently *against* the concept of patterns. I work every day with software that operates at the pattern level when rerouting transit trips. (This happens to also use stop IDs rather than sequence numbers to specify where the reroute occurs within the pattern - the two aspects are somewhat orthogonal.)
https://github.com/conveyal/r5/blob/dev/src/main/java/com/conveyal/r5/analyst/scenario/Reroute.java

However, there is a difference between making a certain choice in the internal data model of one organization's software, and imposing it in a standard used by people around the world for data exchange between disparate tools. The latter requires a different and much stronger argument, as it requires every producer and consumer of that data to implement and support the approach for an unlimited duration of time into the future. It has high collective costs, which may greatly outweigh the costs you or I incur discussing or redesigning it.

My goal here is not to force a different approach just because I have some personal preference for it. I am not arguing that patterns can't be used, or that sequence numbers can't be used, or that stop IDs absolutely must be used in their place. I am, *on a volunteer basis, only providing a review of a proposal,* and making recommendations on how that proposal might be improved before it is submitted to a community for permanent adoption, considering all the downstream effects that might have.

Considering that one goal of Trip-Modifications is to compactly represent changes large numbers of reroutes on similar trips (more compactly than GTFS-NewTrips), looking again at R5 [Reroute.java](https://github.com/conveyal/r5/blob/dev/src/main/java/com/conveyal/r5/analyst/scenario/Reroute.java) that I linked to above, I see a few ideas that could be useful to think about.

R5 Reroute modifications are always applied to entire patterns (to every trip on a pattern at once). Patterns are grouped hierarchically under routes (if the same sequence of stops were to occur on two routes, they would be two different patterns). These patterns can be targeted for modification in two different ways: using either route IDs (select all trips on all patterns on the route) or trip IDs (select all trips on all patterns containing the exemplar trips with the specified IDs). I find the exemplar trip approach to be a very straightforward way to specify and select entire patterns. The sections of the trips to be rerouted are specified with the IDs of the beginning and end stop between which the new section will be inserted, and matched independently to each pattern that was selected. This allows huge numbers of trips to be selected and modified using only a few trip IDs or route IDs, even when those trips are spread across many patterns and the stop sequence numbers are different on each of those patterns. In principle this would work even if the section being replaced was different on each pattern, because only the insertion start and end points are specified. This is more ambiguous than specifying the full list of stops to be replaced as I've suggested above.

I recognize that you want to allow different speeds or timings on different batches of trips, so might not want to select all trips on a route or pattern at once for rerouting. But that is a special case, and people might often want to reroute all trips in the same way (at least during a certain time window). To that end, it would be possible to select routes, patterns (by exemplar tripId), trips (by specific individual tripId) and constrain to time windows. But I do recognize that this is significantly different than the current design of Trip-Modifications which depends on selecting individual trips and specifying only the days on which the detour applies.

Even within a single "system", there are example of non-sequential transfers at the MBTA in Boston whenever we operate free services. Here is one real-world example (references system diagram below) that will be taking place next month due to scheduled track maintenance—@tzujenchanmbd, let me know if you would prefer to consider this out of the current scope since it is within the same agency/feed: - On most evenings, someone boards the Red Line at South Station, alights at Harvard, and transfers to to Route 71 toward Watertown Square for the commute home. - There is allowed a free, single transfer from the Red Line to a bus, with a validity period of 120 minutes from the time of the initial fare validation (at South Station, in this case). - On certain nights, there will be special maintenance during which free buses will replace Red Line train service between Alewife and Park Street. On these nights, someone will board the Red Line at South Station, alight the train at Park Street, board bus from Park Street to Harvard, and finally switch at Harvard to the Route 71 bus. - In this case, the shuttle bus/bus bridge from Park Street to Harvard is free; in fact, no fare validation takes place on this first bus whatsoever. The Red Line and the Route 71 bus both require fare validations as normal. - When boarding the Route 71 bus at Harvard, the transfer from the Red Line at South Station is accepted, and the validity period remains based on the boarding at South Station (rather than the bus bridge boarding at Park Street). From the perspective of the fare system, it is as if the middle leg (bus Park Street to Harvard) never took place.

> > it requires every producer and consumer of that data to implement and support the approach for an unlimited duration of time into the future.
> 
> While this proposal would require the producer to identify patterns to combine trip modifications (or just do one trip modification per trip_id), consumers don't really need to identify patterns. They just need to apply the modification to the list of trips provided by the producer.

My statement is meant to be taken broadly - there is an unbounded future cost to the public associated with standardization decisions, which must be weighed against the current cost of careful design. But looking specifically at just the pattern aspect of this proposal: indeed the consumer can skip validation and match the message to all specified trips without checking that they belong to the same pattern. However, that assigns the more complex part of the work to the producer, which is not consistent with the usual goals of GTFS. 

Interestingly, if validation of the rule is not expected to be enforced at the receiving end, that also raises the question of whether it’s necessary to impose the rule at the sending end. That is, is it necessary to insist on all trips coming from the same pattern? Independently of whether the replacement portion is specified in terms of stop IDs or sequence numbers, and whether it is specified as a full list of stops, a beginning stop and a length, or a beginning stop and end stop, isn’t the only critical thing that the consumer can match that portion-selector to some portion of the trip? Drawing all the trips from the same pattern (as defined in this proposal) is a helpful rule of thumb to guarantee that the message will apply cleanly to all listed trip_ids, but I don't believe it's a necessary condition. There is a comment above that states that patterns as defined in this proposal are the "broadest possible grouping of trips that allows the start and end of each modification to the trip to be unambiguously identified by start stop sequence plus number of stops replaced", but I don’t think this is the case. The broadest group is “trips that contain any stop with the specified sequence number, followed by at least the specified number of stops” (or alternatively, trips that contain the specified stop_id(s), depending on other implementation choices). 

For example, if there were three different patterns that branch out from a common trunk, and all trips on all patterns use the same sequence numbers along that common trunk, a single modification could introduce a detour on the common trunk. The same applies when using stop IDs instead of sequence numbers, but it's even more general.

If the justification for introducing TripModifications (as opposed to a more basic cancel-and-add-trip approach) is to allow producers to compactly and intuitively represent large numbers of detoured trips, the above seems relevant.
