> 
> Another question: Let's say this vendor is hired by a state DOT for a regional project. Could the DOT also vote and cite one of the feeds? That is what I had assumed.

@antrim Yes, this is intended to follow the **"One organization, one feed, one vote"** principle in the voting process. We brought this up in this [comment](https://github.com/google/transit/pull/544#discussion_r2014895280). So your example is spot on.

Also in the [voting requirements ](https://github.com/MobilityData/transit/blob/20250312-New-Governance-proposal/gtfs/Governance/change-process.md#step-24-vote-to-test)of both votes it states: 

> Votes are considered invalid if:
> [...]
> - An individual or organization votes more than once (Only one vote per individual or organization is permitted.)

[Testing requirements ](https://github.com/MobilityData/transit/blob/20250312-New-Governance-proposal/gtfs/Governance/change-process.md#step-24-vote-to-test) should be treated separately. A Producer could use multiple feeds to test as long as it provides proof of testing. 

Do we see a need to improve the language around this? Maybe include the "One organization, one feed, one vote" principle in the voting requirements?

### Documentation overview

> * **Might the volume of documentation and process also pose a barrier to participation?** I suggest an overview might be useful.

Thank you for bringing this up this suggestion. This is something we tried to be mindful of when we drafted this proposal. We had to remove many redundancies to reach this state and to strike a balance between too much and too little information. I think there is value in this type of overview, maybe in the introduction page? Something similar to how we formatted the presentation slides might work well there. 

### Declaration of testers

> * Question: "First Adopters" are testers and would or should declare themselves here?

All proposals are different. Sometimes you know the identity of the testers as of publication of the PR and sometimes someone shows interest in the comments during the discussion. I think this can be flexible as long as it is known before testing.

Here what the proposed governance states on this matter: 

- In the [Pull Request Template](https://github.com/google/transit/issues/543), there is a section dedicated for Testing details highlighting the information needed. 
- During the [discussion period](https://github.com/MobilityData/transit/blob/20250312-New-Governance-proposal/gtfs/Governance/change-process.md#step-22-pull-request-discussion), one of the responsibilities of the Advocate is to update "the proposal’s contents based on the comments received." This would include testing details. If need be, we could be more explicit here about what type of content. 
- Also, in the [testing step](https://github.com/MobilityData/transit/blob/20250312-New-Governance-proposal/gtfs/Governance/change-process.md#step-25-testing), it is the first action of the Advocate to confirm:  "the identity of the [First Adopters](https://github.com/MobilityData/transit/blob/20250312-New-Governance-proposal/gtfs/Governance/roles.md/#first-adopter) which will test the changes and provide commentary in the Pull Request comment section." 

### Higher bar for testing 
> * Why is there a higher bar to test a proposed spec than to adopt?

The goal of this asymmetry in voting thresholds is to build support for a change earlier in the process. When the community backs a proposal before testing begins, contributors may be _more willing_ to take on the risks involved, making it easier to recruit for testing. Placing more importance on early-stage consensus also incentivizes the development of stronger proposals with clearer timelines. 

Additionally, lowering the threshold for the vote to adopt reduces the risk of late reviews and objections undermining the proposal’s original intent after significant resources have already been invested—while still maintaining sufficient oversight to ensure that test outcomes remain aligned with that intent.

> This approach (just as an example) could probably lead to `36 < x < 255` byte IDs but should still be fine.

It would certainly work, and be fine/reasonable by most measures. But considering the file size issues discussed above (as in my comment https://github.com/google/transit/issues/518#issuecomment-2522489082) there might be a real concrete advantage to generating short, purpose-made IDs. Enough of an advantage to avoid the "easy" approach of concatenating a few other IDs, each of which might be a string like `ab73b272ab206fa9466300168527dfa321446c76acc875678e53d90b05fb688f`.

For the specific reason of avoiding unnecessary jumps in file size, I suppose I'm advocating best practices like:
1. Use arbitrary generated IDs of a length adapted to your quantity of entities
2. Order stop_times by trip_id if feasible
3. Expose other info about trips via extension columns in trips.txt (so it won't repeat on every line of stop_times.txt)

Most large GTFS feeds are produced by software systems, not by hand or by hand-written scripts. The existence of best practices could influence or encourage people writing that widely-reused software to choose one approach over another, for reasons they might not think of spontaneously. The developer might be able to very easily produce simple IDs and/or order stop_times on output, but just neglect to do so because no one mentioned this was preferable or advantageous.

To clarify, I do not have an absolute position on "correct" IDs. I just think it is useful to point out implications and make suggestions which help people make informed implementation choices. I can see the appeal of "meaningful" trip_ids made out of other IDs, maybe even advantages in them being naturally persistent across subsequent feed publications. But it is better for file size if they look like `9498_EAST_0645` rather than `1007_117_110_3ANTRAM-23_1128-0710HBK1281_5787_a0126881ee5ec9d45a87041cb8defe97f542a06ad8cad8219ff36d385d338f13`.

In many years of analysing real time feeds the biggest problem I see is that the trip ids don't get transported from the scheduling system to the real time system. Therefore I would not discourage concatenated IDs too much, because it increases the change of the IDs matching as the real time system has a chance to re-generate those lost IDs.

Sure, you could argue that if the IDs get lost they "are doing it wrong" and you would be correct.

If you care about file size (and it would be nice if you did) then nobody is stopping you from using short IDs.

Certainly good points @leonardehrenfried, which could also be mentioned or taken into account in best practices. I mostly just want to avoid people doing things because they weren't aware of the implications or the alternatives.
+1 OpenTripPlanner

@abyrd, you are correct. The original GTFS was just a CSV export of some transit schedule tables from TriMet's in-house developed enterprise database. Many of the base GTFS file names and fields exactly match the table names and columns in our schema.

After an in-depth presentation by MobilityData last week, I feel much better about the overall motivation for the governance changes. I was +0 and I am now +1 about MobilityData's role. I appreciate the delineation between functional, non-functional and documentation changes. Similar to @bdferris-v2, I am +1 for the change in voting process, requiring 2 consumers and 2 producers.

Thank you for the clarifications @antrim and @eliasmbd! I think the language in the Participant Composition sections could be modified a little to further avoid confusion, particularly where it's unclear when Producer/Consumer refers to "producer/consumer of GTFS in general" vs "producer/consumer of the proposed change."

Here's my attempt:

#### Vote to test participant composition
"At least 2 GTFS consumers **and** 2 GTFS producers must participate in the vote.
- Each of these contributors can only be considered either a Consumer **or** Producer, even if they are able to represent both roles.
- First Adopters intending to test the proposal* can vote and count toward this requirement, provided they are not acting as the Advocate for the proposal."

<sub>*I changed the tense of this phrase; it was previously "who tested the proposal" which doesn't make sense since this is the vote *to* test.<sub/>

#### Vote to adopt participant composition
"At least 2 GTFS consumers **and** 2 GTFS producers must participate in the vote.
- Each of these contributors can only be considered either a Consumer **or** Producer even if they are able to represent both roles.
- Consumers and producers do not need to be implementers of the proposed change to count toward this requirement.*
- First Adopters who tested the proposal can vote and count toward this requirement, provided they are not acting as the Advocate for the proposal."

<sub>*Now I'm doubting whether this is actually the case... 😅<sub/>

> Anyway, introducing new Required files/fields or Conditionally Required files/fields based on conditions that are already true for existing feeds would violate backwards compatibility.

@westontrillium Could you clarify what you mean, if, for example, someone wants to propose a new Required or Conditionally Required field? Besides saying it's "confusing" (I mean, c'mon, this is all pretty confusing) what would be the problem with having higher Voting and Testing requirements for changes that would be Required or Conditionally required vs those that would just be Optional or Recommended?

> * **Why is there a higher bar to test a proposed spec than to adopt?** Do I read correctly that testing requires unanimous yes vote but adoption requires 80% yes? Is there some subtle reasoning here?

@antrim thank you for pointing this out. I noticed it too, and figured I was missing the logic behind making it harder to test than to adopt. I would think we would want the exact inverse of that if we want to achieve innovation. 

@eliasmbd I find it hard to interpret the numbers in this proposal as showing that "the community backs" a change or there's "consensus." 

> lowering the threshold for the vote to adopt reduces the risk of late reviews and objections undermining the proposal’s original intent after significant resources have already been invested

@eliasmbd you've essentially expressed the "Sunk Cost Fallacy" here. "Late reviews and objections" should be weighed on their merits, not due to a perception that (A) they're "late" (which they aren't if they're being brought up before a vote to Adopt) or (B) that "significant resources have already been invested." Moreover, I'm surprised you would assume that feedback would challenge the "original intent," but there are plenty of objections someone could raise that challenge not the intent but how well the proposal achieves that intent. 

The likelihood of that is especially higher because of the minimal testing this governance proposal envisions. The more Producers and Consumers involved in Testing, the lower the likelihood of problems being identified just before Adoption or, worse, after Adoption.

> First Adopters

Any objections to calling them "Early Adopters" instead? This may seem "in the weeds," but the contradiction between "First" and there being multiple Adopters is bugging me. The only reason I can imagine to make it singular is if one wanted to limit how many people tested, which the "at least" language indicates is not the intent. This is also a missed opportunity to align with the widely understood Diffusion of Innovation Model.

> "One organization, one feed, one vote:"

Like @antrim this principle was obvious to me. @westontrillium @eliasmbd I'm glad this is now clearly understood. Any other interpretation would concern me, as it would effectively increase the voting power of GTFS vendors while decreasing the voting power of transit agencies. That kind of disenfranchisement would certainly not further MobilityData's goals of engaging more stakeholders. On the other hand, what I'm proposing would structurally incentivize MobilityData's community engagement team, the Advocate, and "First/Early Adopters" to bring more stakeholders into the process.

**"Steward" or "Maintainer"?**

Words matter a lot. I think GTFS needs more than "maintenance" to achieve its full potential. We need "stewardship" of this common resource. That word has some implications I think are relevant to MobilityData's mission:

- Supervising and managing is foundational, but not enough
- Sense of responsibility, duty, accountability, and obligation to the greater good, commensurate with the power endowed with the steward
- There's a connotation that others have placed their trust in the steward
- Brings the gravity of ethics, values and morality to not only _what_ the steward does, but _how_

> Why is there a higher bar to test a proposed spec than to adopt? 

Currently, we ask any first adopters to spend a significant engineering resources, even though any other party can derail the proposal at the vote. This creates a [hold up problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hold-up_problem#:~:text=The%20hold%2Dup%20problem%20is%20a%20situation%20where%20two%20parties,thus%20reduce%20their%20own%20profits.) — that is, one party waits until others have invested, then wields a veto for leverage. The GTFS community context is a bit different, but even if we assume good intention of everyone, the incentive problem stays. 

That's the point of the first vote, which everyone seems to agree on, but we keep the risk if we don't remove the veto power on the second vote.

I can tell you that at Transit we've been burned by [this](https://github.com/google/transit/pull/286#issuecomment-1086446888) [at least twice](https://github.com/google/transit/pull/403#issuecomment-1975320322) that I can remember. And it's not for lack of trying to get feedback before implementation.

> you've essentially expressed the "Sunk Cost Fallacy" here. "Late reviews and objections" should be weighed on their merits, not due to a perception that (A) they're "late" (which they aren't if they're being brought up before a vote to Adopt) or (B) that "significant resources have already been invested."

Any technical objection can still prevail. I don't think the change cheapen merit-based review; it simply prevents a single actor from imposing a huge cost on the entire community.

Classic sunk-cost fallacy focuses on a single actor; here the issue is cross-organisation dynamics, where one late veto can externalise costs onto everyone else. The 80 % rule fixes that.

body:
> @westontrillium Could you clarify what you mean, if, for example, someone wants to propose a new Required or Conditionally Required field? Besides saying it's "confusing" (I mean, c'mon, this is all pretty confusing) what would be the problem with having higher Voting and Testing requirements for changes that would be Required or Conditionally required vs those that would just be Optional or Recommended?

Sure! So GTFS has no versioning, meaning only backwards-compatible changes should be permitted. Since you cannot impose retroactive requirements to the spec, the only backwards-compatible additions that could be introduced are entirely optional files/fields or required/conditionally required files/fields conditioned solely on new optional files/fields included in the same change. For example: A new component couldn't be "conditionally required if shapes.txt is present," because that would invalidate all feeds with shapes.txt that do not add this new component. But, a new component could be conditionally required on the presence of *another* new component introduced in the same change (like levels.txt being required if pathways.txt has an elevator pathway). With this in mind, modifying voting/testing requirements in this way could only be based on "optional" vs "recommended." I've already given my reasons for not introducing new components as "recommended," so to me that only leaves us with one presence category. Perhaps an alternative could be modifying requirements based on the scope of change (e.g., new files vs new fields to existing files only), but I remain hesitant to subdivide further, in keeping with the goal of ensuring the process remains as simple *as possible* (we already have functional vs non-functional, vote to test vs vote to adopt, and the testing requirements themselves...).

> Any technical objection can still prevail. I don't think the change cheapen merit-based review; it simply prevents a single actor from imposing a huge cost on the entire community.

Exactly. I'm not questioning the legitimacy of objections *because* they were made late in a given proposal's journey. Later objections can sometimes lack sufficient context or actually reopen issues already resolved through earlier decisions, BUT there is a strong history of critical modifications coming late in the process that *are* met with assent (e.g., the need to normalize Location Groups in Flex was identified quite close to the Flex vote but something we all eventually strongly supported). The case being made is that the proposed changes attempt to increase the likelihood that those objections are made **as early as possible in the process**—actually to avoid situations where participants are likely to fall into sunk cost thinking.

Yes, there have been discussions for a number of years of adding support within GTFS Realtime alerts to reference pathways, such as escalators and elevators:  https://github.com/google/transit/issues/268

A number of American public transit agencies have plans to implement this, although formally adopting the change into the spec has been waiting on a combo of data producers and consumers to follow through with this.

While it doesn't cover your example, I've been slowly working on adding vehicle.txt to GTFS schedules, which would describe the accessibility features of vehicles. This would link to the vehicle number in the real time data to show features of the approaching vehicle in predictions.

https://github.com/google/transit/issues/458
@ckraatz there's no versioning because that was the default state, there's been [discussions](https://github.com/google/transit/issues/288) about it but no concrete proposal that I know of.

> this is probably a really big topic, but what's the reason GTFS has no versioning?

@ckraatz This has been a big topic indeed. This is partly why we chose to keep the Guiding Principles untouched for now because it is recurring topic and something we might want to touch on in the future after this proposal is voted on. As @gcamp mentioned, I'd invite you to check issue #288 for some additional context. 

> Any objections to calling them "Early Adopters" instead?

We are using "First Adopters" as they have often been referred to as such by the community over the past years. I agree, it is not consistent with the Diffusion of Innovation Model (DIM). Using DIM, it is debatable that they would even be considered "Early Adopters" since that would indicate that we would need between approx. 2.5% and 12.5% of feature adoption in the GTFS market. In DIM, they would actually fall under the "Innovators" category which typically is represented by the first 2.5% of adopters. 

Seen from this perspective, I can understand how it can be confusing. Maybe we should figure out a better name if this is confusing to others too. We do think that being labeled as "First Adopters" can bring some level of recognition to those testing a feature before it even being officially adopted into the specification. Maybe using a more neutral term like "Testers" can work too. 

> "Steward" or "Maintainer"?

The use of the term [Maintainer](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/learning-about-github/github-glossary#repository-maintainer) is a norm on GitHub. This is usually assigned to an individual and sometimes an organization, depending on project size, that is typically responsible for managing the project's code, community, and overall health.

> I can tell you that at Transit we've been burned by [this](https://github.com/google/transit/pull/286#issuecomment-1086446888) [-1 blocker vote] [at least twice](https://github.com/google/transit/pull/403#issuecomment-1975320322) that I can remember. And it's not for lack of trying to get feedback before implementation.

@gcamp Your perspective is really important. We should learn from Transit’s experience as much as possible.

The first example ["[this](https://github.com/google/transit/pull/286#issuecomment-1086446888)"] is a GTFS-Fares v2 base implementation [vote failing in 2021](https://github.com/google/transit/pull/286#issuecomment-997045507) 11 votes in favor, 4 opposed (73% in favor). The spec was [revised by MobilityData](https://github.com/google/transit/pull/286#issuecomment-1026251866) and then [passed in May 2022](https://github.com/google/transit/pull/286#issuecomment-1128856273) with 9 votes in favor and no votes against. There are 184 comments (!) — which I mostly skimmed.

Revisions to the base implementation of GTFS-Fares v2 before a revote depended on MobilityData:

- MobilityData [listed the issues](https://github.com/google/transit/pull/286#issuecomment-1026251866) that motivated opposed votes, and created separate issues to track them.
- MD organized working groups.
- MD revised the GTFS-Fares v2 proposal and then [called a vote](https://github.com/google/transit/pull/286#issuecomment-1080716109).

The success and adoption of GTFS-Fares v2 depended on MobilityData’s facilitation. In the new governance process, do we expect the Advocate would run a similar process when testing reveals the need for changes? 
How do we expect GTFS-Fares v2 would have gone in the new governance process?

>How do we expect GTFS-Fares v2 would have gone in the new governance process?

My expectation is that it wouldn't have changed the length of the discussions and all the work the advocate (MD in this case) would have to do. Having consensus is still a hard process. 

But instead of us going to MD and telling them we were planning to do implement it and implement a draft proposal, we would have saved probably a couple of engineering-week by having the changes done in the first vote discussion before the implementation. 

Even if I agree the testing phase is important and real-implementation are required to show the need for the change is real, it's very rare that there's major changes needed during the testing phase. In both the case of fares-v2 and trip modifications, the changes were based on opinions about implementation detail, not blocker from the point of view of the first adopters. With this in mind, I don't expect changes between the first and second vote to happen often.

## Vote Launch

Hello GTFS Community,

After extending the review period and incorporating some of your feedback, we now feel confident in moving forward with a vote on this proposal. Thank you to everyone who shared their thoughts—any insights not reflected in this version will be collected for future discussions.

### Voting Requirements

As a reminder, here are the voting requirements under the [current GTFS governance](https://github.com/google/transit/blob/master/gtfs/CHANGES.md):

* **Voting duration:** The vote must remain open for at least 14 full calendar days and will close at **23:59:59 UTC** on the final day. The specific end time should be clearly announced at the start of the vote.
* **Allowed changes during voting:** Only editorial revisions (e.g., fixing typos or clarifying wording) are allowed, as long as they do not alter the intent of the proposal.
* **How to vote:** Anyone may vote by commenting on the pull request with a “+1” or “-1.” Votes can be changed during the voting period by editing the original comment (e.g., striking through the initial vote and adding the new one).
* **Timing of votes:** Only votes submitted during the official voting period count. Votes made before the period begins are not considered.
* **Approval criteria:** The proposal is accepted if it receives unanimous “+1” votes  **from at least 3 contributors**, the advocate's vote does not count. 
* **Negative votes:** Must include a reason and, ideally, suggestions for improvement.

### Post-adoption steps

If the new governance is adopted:

* MobilityData proposes the following Adjustment Period:
  * All new PRs opened before adoption (successful vote) of the new governance will be subject to the current governance rules.
  * All PRs opened after adoption (successful vote) of the new governance will be subject to the new governance rules.
* MobilityData proposes to open an issue and/or host a meeting six months after adoption to gather feedback and evaluate how the proposal has been working in practice, determining if a revision is needed.

### Voting Period

We are launching the vote for a period of **16 full calendar days** to take into account the multiple national holidays across the globe. **The vote will close on July 6,  2025 at 23:59:59 UTC.**

Thank you for participating in this process and happy voting!

+1 Trillium

I feel overall quite positive about these changes, and I think the 6 month "trial" period offers us sufficient insurance should there be anything we need to adjust; I'm eager for us to start collectively evaluating how this new process impacts proposals. Thanks to everyone involved for all your contributions on what has been a huge undertaking, and thanks to MobilityData for providing the necessary leadership to keep things moving!

There is no problem here. It indicates that trip A will stop service at 09:00, while trip B will start service at 09:02. There are 2 minutes of downtime where the vehicle is at rest. My suggestion to modify the spec is to not require a departure_time at the final stop and not require an arrival_time at the first stop.

The frontend I am working omits the time from departure boards if it is the final stop of a trip.

> trip A and trip B in the same block
> trip A final stop: stop alpha, arrive 9:00, depart 9:00
> trip B first stop: stop alpha, arrive 9:02, depart 9:02

Since departure at the last stop and arrival at the first stop are redundant, it should be easy to omit them from departure/arrival boards as @miklcct described. In MOTIS we ignore this information completely as it's not required for trip planning nor for any kind of departure/arrival boards and can only lead to inconsistencies.
Shall we make a proposal to make these fields optional?

I guess we've reached the topic of backward compatibility / versioning once more.

As current software (GTFS parsers) might rely on these fields being present/populated *everywhere*, it could mean that a software that's 100% conforming to the current GTFS-standard right now might not be able to parse a GTFS compliant dataset in the future due to missing (optional) values for `arrival_time` and `departure_time`. In my interpretation this change would therefore not be backward compatible.

Since backward compatibility came up already for the `cars_allowed` discussion, and will probably come up more and more, I think it would make sense to have a general discussion about the evolution of the GTFS standard (including GTFS-RT, see `ADDED`). Even if this discussion leads to the consensus that GTFS will never have (semantic?) versioning and we can't make any changes that are not backward compatible, this would still be valuable to know as it would hopefully come with a clear definition of which changes are allowed and which changes are not allowed.

Anyway, I would support making `arrival_time` of the first departure and `departure_time` for the last arrival optional.

> Then I think it is plainly wrong to use the same _route_. I would also argue that in every other standard TER uses they have to split them in two separate lines, which may for the public share the same public code, but never is this thing combined into one timetable.

How about a route which uses a combination of bus and tram vehicles? They all call at the same stops.

> Following here from [#409](https://github.com/google/transit/issues/409), sharing a bit more about the [@mbta](https://github.com/mbta)'s experience with rail replacement buses: > > > Another possibility would be to mark a route to be part/replacement of another route. That way we could link those together and use the information to link the real-time alerts to both routes. > > We are doing exactly this via another extension we designed and implemented, _[multi_route_trips.txt](https://github.com/mbta/gtfs-documentation/blob/master/reference/gtfs.md#multi_route_tripstxt)_. > > In the example below from our [Needham Line route timetable](https://www.mbta.com/schedules/CR-Needham/timetable), Train 839 and Train 841 are actually part of a different `route_id` for the Providence/Stoughton Line (they continue on to another destination beyond Forest Hills), but because the trips are linked to the Needham Line via _multi_route_trips.txt_, we are able to show them on this webpage. > > > A similar treatment is used if, say, a shuttle bus replaced a portion or whole of a Needham Line trip. > > We originally added the `trip_route_type` extension in order to be able to distinguish "replacement bus" trips with normal rail trips on the same `route_id`, however ultimately moved to using separate routes; having trips on both rail and bus `route_id`s stopping at shared `stop_id`s caused issues with more than one feed consumer. Perhaps this could be overcome with an addition to the spec, but backward-compatibility should be considered. > > In our case, using a distinct `route_id` also allows us to give the bus service route/text colors that match the replacing buses, as well as separate route names—particularly useful in situations when a single bus service replaces multiple rail routes. Why do bus and rail sharing a platform cause an issue for your consumers? I think it is the fault of your consumers not handling multi-modal stops correctly. It is common that subway / rail, subway / tram, bus / tram, etc., share platforms.

I think we should continue discussion here as [we have now having problem with NeTEx / GTFS compatibility](https://github.com/opentripplanner/OpenTripPlanner/pull/6676#issuecomment-3018113097).

It is not possible to specify a concept related to passenger information in GTFS compared to NeTEx.

Just for the record an insight. Maybe someone finds this helpful. Let me know if I'm wrong.

The following table shows trip X (from A to B) and Y (from B to C) and their time at those stops (departure time = arrival time to keep it simple). Let's assume there's an in-seat transfer from X to Y at B.

GTFS times:

| trip | A      | B     | C
| -----| ------ | ----- | -----
| X    | 24:00  | 25:00 |
| Y    |        | 00:00 | 01:00

Timezone: Europe/Berlin

Service date:
- 2025-10-25 for X (offset at noon = 2h)
- 2025-10-26 for Y (offset at noon = 1h)


UTC times for these service dates:

| trip | A                 | B                | C
| -----| ----------------- | ---------------- | ----------------
| X    | 2025-10-25 22:00  | 2025-10-25 23:00 |
| Y    |                   | 2025-10-25 23:00 | 2025-10-26 00:00


So in GTFS times it looks like a 23h gap while in UTC there's no gap. This makes it hard to know if the data is correct only by looking at the GTFS times. You need to convert them based on the agency timezone to see if it makes sense. With `block_id` this is easier to detect because every trip within a block has the same `service_id`.

> you can have the same block_id across service_ids

Thanks for pointing it out. That's true and that's also how I implemented it. What I actually meant was that a connection between trips would only occur on "shared service days and block_id". This implies that the same service day results in the same offset to noon for each trip. Therefore, looking at the GTFS times (without translation to UTC) is sufficient to know what's going on. I understand that this trade-off was made in order to enable the "loop trip" use case where a trip has a stay-seated transfer to itself (direct or indirect).

In my previous example, I described the case where the producer created special trips for the DST change day. However, as you said, most producers do not adjust for DST. So a more realistic example could look like this.

GTFS times:

| trip | A      | B     | C
| -----| ------ | ----- | -----
| X    | 24:00  | 25:00 |
| Y    |        | 01:00 | 02:00

Timezone: Europe/Berlin

In general, if both trips are in summer time or both trips are in winter time, it works without problems.

In the DST change case, you could either say it has a 23h offset or just not match them. Not matching them is probably the best option. Shifting the second trip (Y) one hour later in order to try to guess the intention of the producer would be a third option. A best practice could help to deal with those cases.

Service date:
- 2026-03-28 for X (offset at noon = 1h)
- 2026-03-29 for Y (offset at noon = 2h)

UTC times for these service dates:

| trip | A                 | B                | C
| -----| ----------------- | ---------------- | ----------------
| X    | 2026-03-28 23:00  | 2026-03-29 00:00 |
| Y    |                   | 2026-03-28 23:00 | 2026-03-29 00:00


Thank you for pointing me to https://github.com/google/transit/issues/325. I think that more examples and best practices around corner cases (like seated-transfers in connection with DST in this case) or even a test suite could help producers as well as consumers. For example for stay-seated in connection with DST we could:

1. state that producers should introduce special trips (like in my first example) to specifically handle the DST change dates.
2. or alternatively state that producers should *not* introduce special trips for DST change dates (like in this second example) but then we need clearly defined rules how consumers should handle those cases in order to mirror closely what happens in practice.

One issue we've seen is that some agencies use block_id to link multiple trips that don't end start at the same location. In this case, we would want to show a departure from the end stop from the first trip. Admittedly, it doesn't look right because it's in the same stop. 

I'm not against making arrival/departure time optional in the right context, but should we also enforce the first/last stop of a in-seat transfer be exactly the same?

 Right now, block_id don't enforce anything and in-seat transfer via trip to trip transfer has a lax requirement `The last stop of from_trip_id SHOULD be geographically close to the first stop of to_trip_id`.

> but should we also enforce the first/last stop of a in-seat transfer be exactly the same?

+1

> > but should we also enforce the first/last stop of a in-seat transfer be exactly the same?
> 
> +1

When we do interlining, how do we deal with drop_off_type and pickup_type? How should we represent the case where the incoming trip drops off passengers at an alighting only stop, then a new trip is started on another route with 2-minutes changeover time, the vehicle moves forward to a boarding only stop to pick up passengers?

OK. I hadn't realized the flexibility around using block_id.
I can imagine an example:
* A vehicle completes a trip at stop A, the end of the route, arriving and departing at 9:00.
* It goes to some nearby waiting area for a while. Riders cannot stay on the vehicle.
* Then it comes back and starts a new return trip at stop A, arriving and departing at 9:30.

In this example it would be correct to have the same stop and correct to have different times.

This indicates that my first suggestion of requiring that arriving and departing times match wouldn't be correct in every case.

So the real problems with the feed above are:
* It should use transfers.txt to indicate which of these connected trips allow in-seat transfers.
* Less important: It should put accurate arrive and depart times for the stops at transit stations, though correct use of transfers.txt would probably make this less important.

I think we can close this issue as working-as-intended.

I'll think about whether there's a way the validator could detect this "omission of transfers.txt" and create a warning. If I can think of a reasonable approach I'll create a separate issue proposing that.

> When we do interlining, how do we deal with drop_off_type and pickup_type? How should we represent the case where the incoming trip drops off passengers at an alighting only stop, then a new trip is started on another route with 2-minutes changeover time, the vehicle moves forward to a boarding only stop to pick up passengers?

I see two options (in case last stop + first stop have to match):

- If passengers are allowed to stay seated, the part where if moves forward can just be assigned to the first trip (or to the next trip). This probably does not mirror the operational view on those trips and is hard to achieve if the GTFS timetable is a stripped down dump from the operational data. But from a customer / routing perspective this change would do the job.
- If passengers are not allowed to stay seated, it's just two separate trips and no case for `block_id` or `transfer_type=4`.

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/ca90bc2d-940c-48de-92c7-a7d5bfeeb322)

A bit off-topic but there is a complication to this: agencies put block_id into their feeds (for operational reasons, presumably) but it's unclear whether this means that it's a stay-seated transfer or not, because the spec is silent on this topic. You could reasonably assume that it just means that the same bus services multiple trips, nothing else.

HOWEVER, Google does treat block_id as stay-seated: https://developers.google.com/transit/gtfs/examples/block-transfer-example

This is a very unfortunate situation that is quite confusing and I cannot see a good way out. For that reason we (OTP) allow you to configure whether block_id means a stay-seated or not.

IMO the fact that it's the same bus is an operational detail and quoting from the front page of gtfs.org, GTFS is a "standard for **rider-facing** transit information". So any operational detail not relevant for riders (stay seated = relevant, same vehicle without stay seated  = not relevant for riders) should be omitted as there are other standards for this purpose. Some might say that this information is required to propagate delays. However, this is not the job of a GTFS-RT consumer. A proper delay prediction requires way more information than just that and should be done on the GTFS-RT producer side. So again, there's no need to have the "same vehicle" information in GTFS unless it's a stay-seated transfer. My proposal would be to standardize the Google Maps approach of interpreting `block_id` as stay-seated (also because the majority of feeds are tailored to Google Maps anyway and I think this won't change for a long time).
The ability to change pickup_type and drop_off_type has been adopted in #504
+1  from BART

I don't think we can get out of the problematic interpretation of block_id until everyone moves to [trip to trip transfers](https://github.com/google/transit/pull/303) (which is probably never!). Even inside the same feed, some block_id are used as in-seats and others are just vehicle without in-seat transfer. I don't know the details, but I think Google maps also has some heuristics too (or internal configuration?) because some block_id are not shown as in-seat. 

We mentioned it in the original PR but it was a bit hidden : we have a open source [GTFS-blocks-to-transfers](https://github.com/TransitApp/GTFS-blocks-to-transfers) tool that allows you to convert block_id to trip to trip transfers with good heuristics and optional configuration.

Thank you for the link to the block_id converter tool! Somehow I overlooked it.

You are probably right, that some feeds will forever follow the "same vehicle" interpretation which is not helpful for the passenger as it's just an operational detail. I would still say that clarifying the documentation that `block_id` should only be used for *rider-facing* information (i.e. if it means stay-seated) will improve the data quality. The standard should provide guidance for high-quality data. The status quo of the docs is not really helpful in the case of `block_id`.

Just adding the words "where riders can stay seated" would already give data producers clear guidance where to apply `block_id` and where it's not a good idea. Bold text is new:

> A block consists of a single trip or many sequential trips made using the same vehicle **where riders can stay seated** [...].

I would still 100% agree with your forecast: We'll never get writ of this problem completely because many producers don't update their software. But that's only one part of reality. The other part is that we can still improve data quality (and therefore rider information) by having a clear guideline in the documentation.

Even if `block_id` has been replaced by `transfer_type=4` as the best way to describe in-seat transfers, it still supports some other functions:
* `block_id` is used to configure some some real-time systems such as Swiftly
* TODS ([examples](https://github.com/MobilityData/transit-operational-data-standard/blob/main/docs/en/spec/examples.md)) depends on it

I think it would make sense to move away from assuming that block_id implies the availability of in-seat transfers.

Many of these issues were discussed in #32 (discussion from 2016 to 2019).

* [This](https://github.com/google/transit/pull/32#issuecomment-303248307) comment wrestled with clarifying the meaning of `block_id` while preserving backwards-compatibility (imperfectly). It also includes some Slack links and useful inventories of `block_id` practices in real feeds from Interline and Apple.
* [This](https://github.com/google/transit/pull/32#issuecomment-516195678) and subsequent comments addressed this question: _"Should we even allow blocked trips where the last stop of the earlier trip is different than the first stop of the subsequent trip?"_

I wonder if the current use of negative phrasing (e.g., "should not") might come across as a bit strong, especially considering that the final decision rests with data producers. In some regions, producers may have "compelling reasons" (e.g., political considerations).

If you are creating a _standard_ you must use standard language not "do whatever you want to do".

> "Should not" is a phase with a [specific definition](https://gtfs.org/documentation/schedule/reference/#document-conventions) in the standard.

I think "should not" is a good fit here, quoting from RFC 2119:

> **SHOULD NOT**   This phrase, or the phrase "NOT RECOMMENDED" mean that
> there may exist valid reasons in particular circumstances when the
> particular behavior is acceptable or even useful, but the full
> implications should be understood and the case carefully weighed
> before implementing any behavior described with this label.

As background reading material, here is a discussion if having distinct lines and routes in NeTex was a good idea: https://public.3.basecamp.com/p/Cdz5FsVwJRDS61YVsamVBSnP
Looking again at #358, it is still about temporary replacements which is related to this but not the same thing. Despite the lack of traction for this issue, I believe it still stands.

From the NeTEx documentation: > ROUTE is classically used as an interfacing object between operational planning and infrastructure description. `Line` in NeTEx is `routes.txt` in GTFS. And GTFS does not have any concept that mirrors `Route`. On the other hand, all attributes I mentioned such as `route_short_name` and `route_type` are defined on the NeTEx `ServiceJourney` (which is similar to a `trip` in GTFS). So obviously NeTEx can already have separate `OperatorRef`, `TransportMode`, `trainNumbers`, etc., all in the same `Line`. And on top of this, NeTEx has `GroupOfLines` and `Network`. So even if `Route` is not a rider-facing construct (as discussed in the link), NeTEx still has two more grouping mechanisms on top AND the important attributes such as `TransportMode` on the `ServiceJourney` instead of `Line`. So NeTEx would not have this problem we're discussing here for at least two separate reasons not related to `Route`. In general, I see two options: - enable override of all important attributes of `routes.txt` in `trips.txt` (only `route_type` doesn't cover all use cases but would be a starting point) - add another construct on top of route to be able to group routes NeTEx kind of has both. I have no real opinion on what's better - just wanted to mention that there are different options.
I would hope that if we find a modelling to enable this use case here, it also solves the #358 use case and vice versa.

> As background reading material, here is a discussion if having distinct lines and routes in NeTex was a good idea: https://public.3.basecamp.com/p/Cdz5FsVwJRDS61YVsamVBSnP

Route in NeTEx would be Shapes in GTFS
Line in NeTEx would be Route in GTFS

The discussion there is also started by a non-transit expert, that does not appreciate the separation of concerns.

> Shall we close this and merge with [#358](https://github.com/google/transit/issues/358) ?

Terribly sorry, after going through what's going on over there, it actually feels Okay to merge, after all it is calling for the same thing: i.e: specifying transportation mode at trip level... although the initial use case was about a temporary situation.

> In general, I see two options:
> 
>     * enable override of all important attributes of `routes.txt` in `trips.txt` (only `route_type` doesn't cover all use cases but would be a starting point)
> 
>     * add another construct on top of route to be able to group routes
> 
> NeTEx kind of has both.
> 
> I have no real opinion on what's better - just wanted to mention that there are different options.

I suggested your first point in #409 at least for the `route_type` field.

Going back to the original example provided, could this just be incorrect GTFS data creation that's is causing the issue and not anything currently lacking in the spec? Using the example:

> trip A and trip B in the same block
> trip A final stop: stop alpha, arrive 9:00, depart 9:00
> trip B first stop: stop alpha, arrive 9:02, depart 9:02

If the vehicle truly arrives at stop alpha to end a trip at 9:00 and departs at 9:02 to begin another, shouldn't the last stop of trip A be arrive 9:00, depart 9:02, and the first stop of trip B be arrive 9:00, depart 9:02 (i.e., matching arrival and departure times for both)? I ran an example setting it up this way through the Canonical GTFS Schedule Validator and it did not return an overlapping block error from trip A having a departure time *after* trip B's arrival time.

If my assumption is true, perhaps the only remedy needed is adding language clarifying how producers should handle situations where trips sharing a block end and start at the same stop with layover time between the two and **no** non-revenue events in between. Language encouraging the use of `transfer_type=4` to indicate in-seat transfer is rightly already present in the `block_id` field description.

We've always done this as indicated in the original example, and I don't think changing it to this way is necessarily the best way forward:
> shouldn't the last stop of trip A be arrive 9:00, depart 9:02, and the first stop of trip B be arrive 9:00, depart 9:02 (i.e., matching arrival and departure times for both)

I believe from a GTFS/revenue service perspective a vehicle never "departs" from the final stop. It arrives, and then the trip ends. Similarly, the vehicle never arrives at the first stop -- the trip starts and it departs. If we said that the bus departed from both at 9:02, you may end up with it being displayed in an even more confusing way in apps. Today, I believe most of those apps are showing the _arrival_ at the end of the first trip (which is good info if you're on the bus, or waiting for someone to get off, but not as useful if you're waiting for the bus on the next trip), along with the departure on the next trip (which is the thing that's important to you if you're hoping to catch the bus and depart).

I'd probably prefer a spec change to make departure not necessary at the final stop, and arrival not necessary at the first stop, rather than making them match within a stop time or across the two stop times.

I agree with @antrim here:
> I think it would make sense to move away from assuming that block_id implies the availability of in-seat transfers.

"Block" is a term that's so common in the transit industry and its common usage is different than currently defined in the GTFS spec. Changing the definition to match common usage is probably best, otherwise we're fighting everyone's natural inclination.

> Going back to the original example provided, could this just be incorrect GTFS data creation that's is causing the issue and not anything currently lacking in the spec? Using the example:
> 
> > trip A and trip B in the same block
> > trip A final stop: stop alpha, arrive 9:00, depart 9:00
> > trip B first stop: stop alpha, arrive 9:02, depart 9:02
> 
> If the vehicle truly arrives at stop alpha to end a trip at 9:00 and departs at 9:02 to begin another, shouldn't the last stop of trip A be arrive 9:00, depart 9:02, and the first stop of trip B be arrive 9:00, depart 9:02 (i.e., matching arrival and departure times for both)? I ran an example setting it up this way through the Canonical GTFS Schedule Validator and it did not return an overlapping block error from trip A having a departure time _after_ trip B's arrival time.
> 
> If my assumption is true, perhaps the only remedy needed is adding language clarifying how producers should handle situations where trips sharing a block end and start at the same stop with layover time between the two and **no** non-revenue events in between. Language encouraging the use of `transfer_type=4` to indicate in-seat transfer is rightly already present in the `block_id` field description.

So on which trip the bus is on, between 09:00 and 09:02? I think this should be an overlapping block error, as a single bus can't be physically on two different trips at the same time.

I think it's worth noting that SL line 7 is in fact represented as two lines in Transmodel/NOPTIS/NeTEx. This could be do to stopping at different parts of the platform due to differing platform heights and at some stop platforms. Or more likely to assign it to a different GroupOfLines which is used to have it show "Ersättningsbuss" (Replacement buss) instead of "Spårväg city". ``` Spårväg city tram unknown 7 7 Ersätter Spårväg City bus unknown 7 970 ``` Swedish GTFS feeds for trains do also suffer from the issue of having the replacement buses assigned the same route as the trains. So I can certanly see the point of making this change, on the other hand I don't know that it's really accomplices much. A NeTEx Line and GTFS Route would not become anymore interchangeable than they already are. An example of this is SL line 28 which has to be split into route 28, 28X and 28S in GTFS due to the differing route_short_names. GTFS-RT SA still then needs to refer to all there compared to SIRIs 1 Line. Therefore I'm of the opinon that using a GTFS route for conceptual grouping doesn't really work, its more a way of assigning attributes to trips than anything else. Perhaps one solution would be to be able to designate a route as a parent of another one, that way you can have differing route level field values while still being able to tell which is the main one.

> The bus trips of the Stockholm route 7 and the tram trips of the Stockholm route 7 are not in different routes.

The tram line is line 7, the bus line is line 970 designated 7. This PR would not affect this example, since they are different different lines. They are not grouped together either, the bus line belongs to a different group of lines (replacement buses) than the tram line (which is in its own group). It is not technically feasible for us to join these two lines into one GTFS route. From a policy point of view, Trafiklab does not want to deviate from the source structure defined by the PTA when converting to GTFS/NeTEx, which is another reason why we would not implement this. 

From a producer point of view, @Brickblock1 s note on split journeys due to different short_names would be more relevant, and a valid addition to any discussion on routes and trips. I'd say however that the current situation, where we as a producer split transmodel lines into different routes due to different designations is a good thing for data consumers, as these X, S, .., variants of lines are often treated as different lines when communicating with travellers.

Do you mean that the bus below is actually on line 970? It is mixed between the tram departures.

![image](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/1e/SL_line_7_bus.jpg)

The above is not a replacement bus for tram line closure. It is run in addition to the trams.

That bus is technical line 970, designated 7 (in the same way one agency can have "bus line 1" in 5 different cities by using different technical line numbers, for example 1, 101, 201, 301, 401). The bus shown in the picture is, in the PTA data, on a different line than the trams. The bus is replacement/reinforcement traffic making up for a lack in available seating on the trams compared to the expected number of riders. They usually are used as replacement buses, but during the summer months they are scheduled continuously. Given that the replacement bus line already exists, it likely makes more sense (and is technically/operationally easier) to run the reinforcement traffic on the replacement line. Additionally, the reinforcement traffic is using the replacement bus line color. This means that, if the color were to be included in the GTFS feed, there would be a need for two different routes with their own `route_color`. even if route types could be defined on trip level. A deviation message is available in the realtime feed, and on the [PTA website](https://sl.se/reseplanering/trafiklaget?locationType=LINE&name=Sp%C3%A5rv%C3%A4g+city&number=7&designation=7&transportType=TRAM&transportSubType=SPARVAG_CITY&start=T-Centralen&end=Waldemarsudde).

> That bus is technical line 970, designated 7 (in the same way one agency can have "bus line 1" in 5 different cities by using different technical line numbers, for example 1, 101, 201, 301, 401). The bus shown in the picture is, in the PTA data, on a different line than the trams. > > The bus is replacement/reinforcement traffic making up for a lack in available seating on the trams compared to the expected number of riders. They usually are used as replacement buses, but during the summer months they are scheduled continuously. Given that the replacement bus line already exists, it likely makes more sense (and is technically/operationally easier) to run the reinforcement traffic on the replacement line. Additionally, the reinforcement traffic is using the replacement bus line color. This means that, if the color were to be included in the GTFS feed, there would be a need for two different routes with their own `route_color`. even if route types could be defined on trip level. > > A deviation message is available in the realtime feed, and on the [PTA website](https://sl.se/reseplanering/trafiklaget?locationType=LINE&name=Sp%C3%A5rv%C3%A4g+city&number=7&designation=7&transportType=TRAM&transportSubType=SPARVAG_CITY&start=T-Centralen&end=Waldemarsudde). Thanks. This is convincing enough for me they are operationally two different routes, but this runs against the GTFS Best Practice that > All trips on a given named route should reference the same route_id. > Different directions of a route should not be separated into different route_id values. > Different spans of operation of a route should not be separated into different route_id values. i.e. do not create different records in routes.txt for “Downtown AM” and “Downtown PM” services).
It does not go against the GTFS Best Practice, because GTFS does not allow a route to be multi modal.
However it is extremely confusing to passengers if there are two different routes with the same public code in the same geographical area.
Passengers have absolutely 0 to do with routes.txt.

> Passengers have absolutely 0 to do with routes.txt.

It will result in your journey planner telling your partners to take _route 7 or route 7_ (with different background colours) to your destination, if both route 7 and route 7 serve the journey, and that becomes confusing.

It won't.
 1. If the operator chose the same name, why wouldn't they choose the same colours? 
 2. Generally don't operate on the same time (unless the new trips are actually reinforcement trips), they they don't compete.
 3. Routes never compete, trips compete.

> > As background reading material, here is a discussion if having distinct lines and routes in NeTex was a good idea: https://public.3.basecamp.com/p/Cdz5FsVwJRDS61YVsamVBSnP
>

Thanks for nominating an expert in non-transit matters. But I agree that these are two are completely different discussions. The basecamp post is not relevant to this discussion.

> Thanks for nominating an expert in non-transit matters. But I agree that these are two are completely different discussions. The basecamp post is not relevant to this discussion.

Nobody takes away your data hustling qualities!

The question of temporary bus routes is not at the core of the issue we had. The simple case was that when there was a replacement bus service, it acted in place of the train line, i.e. its the same line. This had various implications for presentation and ticketing, as well as data creation and delivery. The solution was to build them as a single NeTEx Line instead of doing duplicates. There were some intricate details that spoke for that solution. But of course, we re-publish all input-data as both NeTEx and GTFS, and its not always easy to recreate these more detailed NeTEx solutions in the GTFS format. So, temporary or permanent. Doesnt matter, the issue remains the same.

So, I believe these two matters speak to the same usecases and solutions. The two issues can be merged (whichever direction).

I actually heard of a boat line in Norway where the last bit was so annoying to go around, especially in rough seas, so the captain just had a minibus at the second to last quay, and finished the trip by road :)

body: I'm going to call for a vote. The voting period will end on Aug 21, 2025 at 23:59:59 UTC.
-1 OpenGeo
+1 MOTIS

The alternative would be that consumers create this artificial node internally (which could also be made a "best practice").

Since MOTIS currently does not do this, we would definitely benefit from the best practice you propose.

If the majority of consumers would not handle the Variant A correctly, the question is: why only a best practice and not a requirement in the spec?

The distance of 2m is very strict. In most cases, a higher distance would still work (depending on the use case).

@skinkie As far as I understand the specifications, `shape_dist_traveled` can use any unit. So having a direct distance of 1000 meters, while the difference between both shape points is 2000 should be totally fine. I'm not even sure, the "distance" needs to be consistent on one trip. (At least I didn't read anything about that.)

I'm not sure, if I understand example 2 correctly, as we only know two shape points and nothing in between. (If we would know more, there had to be more point as well.) So the only assumption we can make is, that any stop on that segment needs to on the direct connection between those. Using `shape_dist_traveled`, we can interpolate and guess its location. But I would prefer, if there were any shape points nearby. Making it a requirement would therefore help us, too.

@MichaelKutzner think implementations can do a lot of things, like taking the nearest shape point before the stop, and draw a straight line from stop location, do an nearest point to the linestring. All fine for me, but I hope that everyone would agree it would get a lot easier if stop-to-stop shapes.txt would be the result of this change.

> I am all for making this a requirement in the spec, but the 2 meter would be a best practice.

I agree with both:

- spec: there should be at a minimum of one shape point associated with one stop in the proximity of the respective stop
- best practice: proximity = <2min

+1 Transit

@skinkie are you suggesting we don't mention open data best practices in the GTFS best practices at all, or that we should re-use existing open data best practices? Tried to look and [The Open Definition](https://opendefinition.org/) looks like it's the closest to what GTFS needs, but it's also very broad and strict, probably stricter that we need it to be.

@gcamp either we follow strict "open data" rules / best practices. Or we stick with being a transit standard. While most of us share the first goal (too), we are here for a transit standard.

Using git blame I cannot see where this line actually came from "The URL should be directly accessible without requiring a login to access the feed." but it is also an _open activism_ claim.

Do you have examples where it's reasonable to have stops relatively far away from the shape? 

I can't think of an example but open to be proven wrong. I'm also assuming : 
- the shape is where the vehicle travels 
- the stop location is where riders and board/alight the vehicle. The stop location should not be 1) the center of a station (that should be a `location_type=1` 2) entrance location (should be `location_type=2`). 

I think 2m is very small and should be expanded. The quite common and valid case of shape going in the middle of the street and stop on the curb doesn't fit that 2m requirement.
+1 Transitous

@gcamp examples where the shape point is independent of the stop are plenty. I have personally solved these cases by assuming that to shape points form a line, and, if no distance is available, the stop can be projected orthogonality to that segment, otherwise it is projected towards the same shape_dist_traveled.

I guess in Europe 2 meters should work, as the width of the road is 3.25-3.50m, center would then be 1.75m from the curb.

> [@MichaelKutzner](https://github.com/MichaelKutzner) think implementations can do a lot of things, like taking the nearest shape point before the stop, and draw a straight line from stop location, do an nearest point to the linestring. All fine for me, but I hope that everyone would agree it would get a lot easier if stop-to-stop shapes.txt would be the result of this change.

I agree, there are many things implementations can do. I just wanted to make clear, that we are missing information in these cases and then have to make a guess, that can be arbitrary wrong.

@natekauf there definitely is an ambiguity between both cases when representing `NO_SERVICE` alerts in GTFS-RT.

TLDR:

- `NO_SERVICE` should be clarified in the spec. Usually, it means that the station (or the platform) is closed and the train will not run through it. It is different to a station bypass.
- The current spec can handle a station bypass by indicating through informed entities that there is no service to the entrances and exits of a platform that is bypassed. A less-than-ideal solution for now.
- It might be possible to introduce an effect like `STATION_BYPASS` which indicates that a train is running through but not stopping at stations. This is to remove confusion around `NO_SERVICE` for station-based routes.

---

We tried to represent both cases using the current GTFS-RT capabilities.

Usually (in real-world cases), `NO_SERVICE` alerts for trains mean that the train will not pass through the stations (that a segment is closed). By this assumption, a possible way of differentiating between both cases is:

**Case 1: Service suspension in both directions between specific stations**
Initially, we can set up

```
“informedEntities”: [
{“stopId”: “stop_3_1”,},
{“stopId”: “stop_3_7”,},
{“stopId”: “stop_4_1”,},
{“stopId”: “stop_4_7”,},
{“stopId”: “stop_5_1”,},
{“stopId”: “stop_5_7”,},
]
```

The `route_id` and `direction_id` can also be specified if the `stop_ids` are not split by direction.

The segment from station 3 to 5 is closed. However, the riders should be able to:

- Board the train at stop_3_1 to go to station 1.
- Exit from the train at stop_3_7 coming from station 1.
- Board the train at stop_5_7 to go to station 7.
- Exit from the train at stop_5_1 coming from station 7.

So practically, only **station 4** is closed and unreachable. Each `stop_id` (platform) in the limit stations 3 and station 5 is actually used (Eg. The rider cannot use stop_5_7 if they come from station 1 because the train will stop at station 3. However, the rider can use stop_5_7 if they are starting at station 5 and going to station 7.)

For this to work in GTFS-RT, all stops of station 3 and station 5 should NOT be included.

```
“informedEntities”: [
{“stopId”: “stop_4_1”,},
{“stopId”: “stop_4_7”,},
]
```

This tells the consumer that all platforms in station 4 are closed. From a routing POV, a trip planner should be able to route the rider to station 3 if they come from station 1, but it should not be able to do so when coming from station 7.

Note: Sometimes consumers use informedEntities to show the alert to the user on a station-level. ie. When planning a journey at station 5, the user would see the alert, despite Station 5 not being closed. In that case, another passive alert (eg. effect=OTHER_EFFECT) can be set up including the limit stations 3 and 5 only, just to inform the user.

**Case 2: Bypassed stations (train runs but does not stop)**
```
“informedEntities”: [
{“stopId”: ..,}
… (all the ids for exits and entrances to the impacted stations).
]
```

When the informed entities say that the access is blocked to stations through closing exits and entrances, consumers can interpret this as: there is service (train is passing) between stations 3 and 5 but the rider cannot go inside the stations or exit them.

In this case, there is no need to think about boundary stations because each of the bypassed stations behaves similarly.

In both cases, the boundary stations can be handled with the current spec. But the issue resides in having to use hackish methods to indicate a station bypass effect.

body: +1 SkedGo
+1 Aubin

Thank you for the thoughtful response, @skalexch!

> Note: Sometimes consumers use informedEntities to show the alert to the user on a station-level. ie. When planning a journey at station 5, the user would see the alert, despite Station 5 not being closed. In that case, another passive alert (eg. effect=OTHER_EFFECT) can be set up including the limit stations 3 and 5 only, just to inform the user.

The prospect of creating multiple alerts for one service disruption is briefly discussed above. We feel strongly that this wouldn't be an ideal way to handle this situation, because it implies that there is more than one disruption occurring when there is not (there is no official way to "link" alerts as relating to the same disruption). A full list of alerts along the route / route status (e.g. https://www.mbta.com/schedules/CR-Fairmount/timetable) would include multiple alerts for the single disruption, leading to undue confusion and concern about how disrupted the route truly is.

> When the informed entities say that the access is blocked to stations through closing exits and entrances, consumers can interpret this as: there is service (train is passing) between stations 3 and 5 but the rider cannot go inside the stations or exit them.
> 
> In this case, there is no need to think about boundary stations because each of the bypassed stations behaves similarly.
> 
> In both cases, the boundary stations can be handled with the current spec. But the issue resides in having to use hackish methods to indicate a station bypass effect.

It does seem like adding `activities` to `informed_entities` with stops would make the situation you describe above much clearer for consumers. Adding a `STATION_BYPASS` effect is probably a good idea too.

The big elephant in the room for this proposal, to me, is that—as far as I understand—it’s mainly intended for behavior change rather than for information display to the user. And using alerts for behavior change is not something that’s [been agreed upon](https://github.com/google/transit/issues/469).

We can debate whether NO_SERVICE should be used in this way or not, since it’s already used like this in practice. However, it seems to me that introducing new alert features specifically aimed at behavior change should instead be handled more explicitly within the existing Trip Updates / Trip Modifications spec.

We use the `cause` values but minimally. It will change some fallback values when other fields are not present (like the description), and will allow us to provide a more detailed summary (before the user seeks the full alert content). 

I see no problem with the proposal and support it. 👍

We've had a few agency customers ask us to add this to the list of causes we offer in our software, not understanding that the causes are defined by a specification and not just product features we unilaterally decide. 

This is the one and only new cause we've ever had requests for, and we've had it multiple times from different agencies. It's the one major hole I see in the current list and I'm in favor of adding it.

We enhance agencies' gtfs-rt alert feeds and add causes derived from descriptions. We do this to allow clients to display e.g. symbols representing the alert type or give better summaries.

Concerts and events (e.g. sports events like football games) have been categories we until now explicitly assigned to `OTHER_CAUSE`. `SPECAL_EVENT` would indeed be a good addition and cover > 90% of the OTHER_CAUSE.

Regarding the question "other use cases for the new category", I suggest to broaden "marathon" to sports events, or add "or other sports events". Such events may result in positive effects like additional services, 

Less than 10% of our category "OTHER_CAUSE" are short term staff shortages or natural disasters (some of the latter we assign to WEATHER).
Many of our users expressed this lack as well in the list of causes, and many current uses of `OTHER_CAUSE` are indeed "special events" of the described types.

Support resources from the first adopters are ready. We plan to initiate a vote on this PR on Sep 8. Dataset and trip planner implementation screenshots will be attached when initiating the vote.

Producer: Public Transportation Open Data Center (ODPT, Japan)
Consumer: Google Maps

Side note: this PR is the first step of the [3-phase plan](https://github.com/google/transit/issues/438#issuecomment-2289511429), not trying to solve all station modeling issues.
I agree with @nkemphues that converging on meters would be best, but adding a unit field seems more practical, at least for now.
Disagree, that would mean there _is_ flexibility, and everyone from that point on **must** implement it.

Thank you all for your contributions.
The voting period ended on Aug 21, with 6 votes in favor and 1 vote against. @skinkie, does @westontrillium’s statement above make sense to you?

Thanks for raising this @ckraatz.

First, we want to clarify that the new [GTFS Schedule governance](https://github.com/google/transit/blob/master/gtfs/Governance/introduction.md) and the [GTFS Realtime Specification Change process](https://github.com/google/transit/blob/master/gtfs-realtime/CHANGES.md) are two separate processes. Since this change impacts GTFS Realtime, we have to work with the current rules that govern GTFS Realtime changes. 

That said, we recognize this process is far from perfect and has many areas for improvement (including the language/terminology used, as you’ve pointed out.) Historically, though, the community has followed a consistent process that looks like the following. I’ll ask you to refrain from over-reading the wording of steps, as they’re meant to be an overview of the relevant steps, not the exact process. 

1. A PR is opened and announced on the GTFS Realtime Mailing List (Which You’ve Done)  
2. The community engages in a discussion period to provide feedback, which should last at least 7 days (This is our current stage).  
3. After the discussion period, one Producer and one Consumer implement and test the proposal and share their results (Yet to take place)  
4. After results have been shared, the advocate can call for a vote. This period lasts at least 7 days.
   1. Official adoption into the spec requires a minimum of 3 Yes (+1) votes. However, a single No (-1) vetoes the proposal.
   2. Experimental adoption has a lower threshold for approval \- 80% of the votes are in favour. Then, you have 2 years to get the change officially adopted (through a unanimous vote).
   3. In any scenario, everyone is welcome to vote.

This is how the community implements the voting and change process for Realtime. Though, I invite any community members to chime in if I’m missing anything or have misrepresented the process. 

There are definitely gaps and areas for improvement in this process, and there may be value in the future to consolidate them or at least bring the RT process closer to parity in terms of robustness and clarity to the new GTFS Schedule governance. But for now, they remain separate.

As for the matter of enforcement, while MobilityData plays an active role in fostering a healthy discussion space and monitoring that the community follows the rules agreed upon, any contributor is capable of speaking up if they believe the process isn't being followed correctly. **In practice, the process is based on discussion and mutual accountability to maintain trust, clarity, and collaborative decision-making.** 

**GTFS is community-driven specification, so it relies on healthy discussion where the advocate should work towards building consensus and trust rather than “win” arguments.** Disagreements are natural, but we want to encourage contributors to engage constructively and respectfully so that this discussion translates into changes that deliver value for everyone using GTFS.

When discussions risk reaching a dead end, the best next step is often to bring in more voices from the community for additional input and perspective. We’d recommend that approach here to help move the discussion forward.

As an agency that must accommodate numerous special events (like parades, street festivals, triathalons, etc.) throughout the year, we feel this is an important enough and frequently-used enough category that it's worth distinguishing from `other_cause`. For what it's worth, sometimes detours and other disruptions caused by special events can be the most impactful to the network than any other cause that's commonly used (like construction or weather). > We automate service alerts as much as possible, but realistically there are so many unique scenarios that GTFS-realtime Service Alerts requires human intervention. Yes, that reflects operational reality. Sometimes there are flag stops, sometimes there's a shuttle between stations and some agencies call it a "bus bridge," one of our customers gives riders Uber vouchers when a train is canceled.
> 
> I wonder in The Hague what percentage of alerts are either created manually/ad hoc or would benefit from being created that way because the automated version is lacking in essential information.
> 
> I get the sense you'd like to replace GTFS-realtime with Siri because Siri is better. If that's your stance, pushing that agenda in every minor GTFS-realtime change doesn't seem constructive or pragmatic.
>
